Proposition 2.3 needs only an R_∞ ⊗ S_N-module structure; (5a) uses the diamond compatibility, which is stated; (5b) needs only T^an-equivariance, since the R_Q-action factors through traces, and Lemma 3.5 provides it. The final conclusion uses R^min ↠ T_{∅,m∅}, where Q = 1 and there are no U_x.
So this is a genuine but minor gap: a step asserted with an insufficient citation. The mathematics is right as intended. Defence tried and fails. By §3.2.4, T_{Q_N} = T is generated over O by T_n, the diamond operators ⟨a⟩ and U_x for x|Q_N. So surjectivity needs U_x in the image of R_{Q_N}. From Theorem 3.11 as printed, the image contains the following. (a) Traces: tr ρ′_Q(Frob_ℓ) = T_ℓ·η(Frob_ℓ). (b) The values of ξ on D_x: the universal representation splits at x as χ_α ⊕ χ_β over R_{Q_N}, and ξ is the image of χ_α. (c) Hence the Δ_{Q_N} diamond operators, by the I_x compatibility. (d) Hence η, a p-power-order function of those diamond operators, and so every T_ℓ. U_x is not reached. On forms whose Δ_x-character is nontrivial, ρ_Q is ramified at x, so no trace of a Frobenius lift equals U_x. Theorem 3.11 fixes ξ(Frob_x) only mod m ("ξ̄(Frob_x) ≡ α_x mod m"), and the diamond compatibility is only for ξ|I_x. Nothing else in §3 closes the gap. Lemmas 3.5 and 3.6 get U_x from T^an by Hensel only at Γ_0(Q) level, where U_x² − T_xU_x + x⟨x⟩ = 0. A characteristic-0 argument (T^an determines the eigensystem) is not available either, because weight-one H^0 can have torsion that does not lift, which is the point of the paper. Remark 3.12's "the required information is preserved under congruences" covers only what the theorem states. §5 shows the authors knew the step is needed. Conjecture A(3) includes U_x = T_{π_x} in the local character φ, and Lemma 5.6 then argues explicitly "by Hensel's Lemma … the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces" before claiming R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} in Thm 5.11. §3 has no such argument. So this is a step asserted without adequate proof, a gap. Consequences: surjectivity is never used. The R_∞-action on H_N only needs some homomorphism. Condition (5a), first part, needs the S_N (Δ_N-diamond) image inside the image of R_∞, which comes from the I_x compatibility in Thm 3.11. Its second part is argued from χ_{α_x}|I_x and R_{Q_N}/aug = R^min. (5b) and (5c) use Lemmas 3.5/3.7 and Prop. 3.8. The proof of Prop. 2.3 (p. 312) never uses surjectivity onto a Hecke algebra. Theorem 3.26's conclusion needs surjectivity only for Q = 1 (R^min ↠ T_∅,m∅), and T_∅ has no U_x. Theorem 3.30, which repeats this proof, and §4 add no dependence on it. The claim is also true, by standard local-global compatibility transported from weight n.

sourceIssues.printed: We claim that U_x ∈ T_{∅,m_∅} for all x|N. This is a consequence of the assumption that N(ρ̄) = N as we now explain. Suppose that x‖N. sourceIssues.correction: Split the cases by whether ρ̄^{I_x} is zero, not by the exponent of x in N. (1) If ρ̄^{I_x} ≠ 0, it is a line. This always happens when x‖N. By the standing hypothesis of §3.1 it also happens whenever ρ̄|G_x is reducible, including cases with x²|N, e.g. ρ̄|G_x ≅ μ ⊕ μχ with χ wildly ramified. In this case the paper's own argument works: the minimal representation into GL_2(T_m) has a unique invariant T_m-line (Def. 3.1(4)) on which Frob_x acts by U_x, so U_x ∈ T_m. (2) If ρ̄^{I_x} = 0, which is equivalent to ρ̄|G_x being irreducible and forces x²|N, then U_x = 0. The conclusion U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} for all x|N still holds, and so does the rank-one claim. This correction is right and minimal: it changes only which condition labels the two cases.

Minimal deformations have det equal to the Teichmüller lift of det ρ̄, and their I_x-invariants are a rank-one direct summand when ρ̄|G_x is reducible. The conductor exponent at x is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan. So x‖N does imply dim ρ̄^{I_x} = 1, but x^2|N does not imply ρ̄^{I_x} = 0: a 1-dimensional invariant space with a wild complementary character gives exponent ≥ 2. I redid the counterexample. On F_49^×, ψ̄^c = ψ̄^7 = ψ̄^{-1} ≠ ψ̄, so ρ̄ = Ind ψ̄ is irreducible. It is odd (det(c) = χ_{-4}(c) = -1) and unramified at 3. It lies on X_1(196)/H and reduces to ρ̄, since η ≡ 1 mod 3. Its a_2 = ψ((1+i))η(2) is a root of unity. So U_2 acts on H^0(X,ω)_{m_∅}, and on the reduction in H^0(X,ω_k(-∞))[m_∅], by a unit, although 4|N. It does not force x‖N, because the conductor exponent is codim ρ̄^{I_x} + Swan, and Swan is positive when the ramified character is wild. For x = 2 this is possible for every odd p, since χ_{-4} is ±1-valued.

- Take p = 3, K = Q(i), and ψ' the order-4 character of the ray class group mod 7 of K, i.e. of F_49^×/μ_4 ≅ Z/12.
- Computed facts: ψ' is trivial on the units and on the image of Z, so it gives an order-4 ray class character. ψ'^c = ψ'^7 = ψ'^{-1} ≠ ψ'. ψ'^2 = χ_{-7}∘N. ψ'((1+i)) = −1 (a root of unity for any choice).
- ρ̄ = Ind_K^Q ψ̄' has these properties:
  - It is absolutely irreducible and odd, with det = χ_{-4}.
  - It is unramified at 3.
  - It stays irreducible over Q(ζ_3), since the quadratic fields in Q(i, √−7) do not include Q(√−3).
  - At 7 (7 ≡ 1 mod 3, so not vexing), ρ̄|G_7 is irreducible and ρ̄|I_7 = ψ̄' ⊕ ψ̄'^{-1}, so the exponent is 2.
  - At 2, ρ̄|G_2 ≅ μ ⊕ μχ_{-4}. This is reducible, with a 1-dimensional invariant line, and χ_{-4} is wild, so the exponent is 1 + 1 = 2.

- The theta series θ_{ψ'} is a weight-1 newform of level 196 with nebentypus χ_{-4}, which is trivial on H. It therefore lies in H^0(X,ω)_{m∅}. Its U_2-eigenvalue is a_2 = ψ'((1+i)) = −1, which is nonzero mod 3. So "x²|N ⇒ U_x = 0" is false.

- Lift by Deligne–Serre to a characteristic-0 eigenform g of weight p and level N. It is new, because N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_g) | N.

- Theorem 4.8 does not use it. The §3.9.2 rank-one remark is only for the characteristic-0 case, via multiplicity one.
- With the corrected split, U_x ∈ T_{∅,m∅} still holds for every x|N, so the side claim survives. Only the proof step is wrong.

sourceIssues.correction: Justify local–global compatibility at x‖N for U_x. Let A ≡ 1 mod ϖ^m lift a power of the Hasse invariant. Multiplication by A embeds H^0(X, ω_{O/ϖ^m})_{m∅} injectively into H^0(X, ω^n_O)_{m∅}/ϖ^m. The embedding respects T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ Np), the diamond operators and U_x for x|N, because on q-expansions mod ϖ^m it is the identity and U_x acts by a_j ↦ a_{jx} in every weight. In weight n, every eigenform f in the m∅-part has level N with N(ρ̄) | N(ρ_f) | N, so f is new at x. This is where N(ρ̄) = N is really used. By Carayol, U_x f is the Frob_x-eigenvalue on the line ρ_f^{I_x}. The weight-n Hecke algebra T^an_{n,m∅} is O-flat and becomes a product of fields after inverting p (strong multiplicity one for newforms), and ρ_n^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. So the Frob_x-eigenvalue λ_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅} on that summand equals U_x. Hence U_x ∈ T^an_{n,m∅}, and its image gives U_x ∈ T_m. The case m = 1 already gives what the rank-one argument needs. The candidate's correction is this argument and is correct. The one point it should state explicitly is the newness at x of every weight-n form, which gives both the reducedness it invokes and Carayol's formula.

Defence attempted. Nothing in the paper supplies the Frobenius/U_x identification for x|N.
(1) Theorem 3.11 ('Local–Global Compatibility', p. 323) gives only three things: traces T_x for x ∤ pNQ, minimality outside Q, and the local shape at x|Q. For x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄), minimality (Definition 3.1(4)) says only that ρ^{I_x} is a rank-one direct summand. It says nothing about which element of T acts on it by Frob_x. So existence and uniqueness of the line are supplied, but 'Frob_x acts by U_x' is not.
(2) U_x for x|N is not even in the paper's Hecke algebras. T and T^an_n are generated by T_ℓ (ℓ ∤ NQp), the diamond operators, U_x for x|Q and U_p (pp. 314–315, 327). So Theorem 3.14 ([15, Lemma 5.1.1], Carayol) and the proof in §3.5 transfer only conditions (2) and (4) to weight one, not any U_x-compatibility.
(3) Remark 3.12 describes the Hasse-invariant congruence method only for x|Q. It is the right tool here, but the paper never applies it to x|N.
(4) In the 'finite case' (H_0(X, ω_K)_{m∅} = 0) there are no characteristic-0 weight-one forms, so compatibility must be proved for a torsion, possibly non-reduced T_m. The paper itself stresses that such local–global compatibility for weight-one Katz forms over Z_p-algebras 'is non-trivial, and requires us to prove' it (p. 298). So the one-line assertion is a step without proof or citation, which is a gap under PROTOCOL §18.
The assertion is nevertheless true, by the argument in the correction; I checked each step. One check was that I_x-invariants of the minimal ρ commute with base change here: when x‖N, ρ̄|I_x is either 1 ⊕ ψ with ψ of prime-to-p order or non-trivial unipotent, and in both cases the rank-one summand persists in quotients. Theorem 1.4 as stated (R^min ≅ T_m and H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m free, with no rank) does not use it. Corollary 1.5 does not use it, and nothing later cites it. sourceIssues.correction: Give every x ∈ S(ρ̄) − T(ρ̄) the group of the P-bullet: U_x = V_x = { g ∈ GL_2(Z_x) : g ≡ (∗ ∗; 0 d) mod x^{c_x}, d ∈ (Z/x^{c_x})^× of p-power order }. They are congruent mod m. Their nebentypus changes by χ^{2j}, which has nontrivial 3-part, so they appear on the printed X_U. Their T_ℓ eigenvalues differ: take ℓ split in Q(i), with a_ℓ ≠ 0 and χ(ℓ) ≠ 1.
- The normalising twist of Thm 3.11 has η = χ^{-j}, the unique p-power square root of χ^{-2j}. So all three forms give the same point of R^min, and φ: R^min → T_{∅,m∅} is not surjective.
- To make T ≠ ∅, so that Theorem 3.30 (p. 350) itself fails, also ramify ψ tamely at 23. This prime is inert in Q(i) and 23 ≡ −1 mod 3; use an order-4 character trivial on μ_4 and nontrivial on μ_24, so 23 is vexing. χ is unramified at 23, so the twists keep the inertial type there and stay σ-isotypic.

(b) Reading "reducible" as "ρ̄|I_x reducible" does not save the text. For odd x with ρ̄|I_x irreducible (wild dihedral case) the same failure occurs. Example: p = 3, ρ̄ = Ind from Q(√−7) of an order-7 ray class character of conductor 𝔭_7² (the ray class group has a Z/7 quotient). Complex conjugation acts by −1 on (1+𝔭)/(1+𝔭²), so ρ̄|I_7 is irreducible. Here c_7 = 3, (Z/343)^× has 3-part Z/3, and cubic twists keep the conductor at 7^3.

This also refutes H-part1a-8's claim that S − (T ∪ P) would then contain only x = 2.

Why the paper's argument breaks: in §3.8 (p. 339), φ is "easily seen to be surjective" only because X = X_1(N)/H kills the p-power diamond operators. Then η = 1 and T is generated by the images of the traces. Theorem 3.30's proof says it "is the same as the proof of Theorem 3.26", with ρ'_Q := ρ_Q ⊗ η "defined as before" (item (4), p. 353). With the printed U, η is nontrivial and surjectivity fails.

Nothing nearby supplies the missing quotient. The only uses of P(ρ̄) are the U-bullets and the cusp remark ("∏_{T} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{P} Z_x^× acts transitively", p. 351). Enlarging the group there to ∏_{S−T} Z_x^× only helps transitivity, so the correction is compatible with it.

The P/non-P split looks deliberate, so the intended group is not clear from context. It is an error, not a misprint. X-K4-2's correction and the earlier verdict on H-part1a-8 agree with mine, and theirs is the minimal change. H-part1a-8's first fix (the I_x reading) is insufficient, as shown in (b); its alternative fix (p-power d at every x in S − T) is correct.

Since 𝓛_{σ,x} is finitely generated and Ô_{X,x} is faithfully flat over 𝒪_{X,x}, 𝓛_{σ,x} is flat and therefore free. The candidate's proposed correction is right and minimal. sourceIssues.reason:
I transcribed the text from a 200 dpi render of p. 346. The proof speaks of "stalks at points of X − Y", L_{σ,x} and O_{X,x}, so the rings are Zariski local rings; Lemma 3.28 separately says "along the formal completions at x" when it means completions. For a finite map f, the Zariski stalk (f_*O_{X(V)})_x is the semilocal ring of X(V) along the fibre over x. It equals ⊕_{x′↦x} O_{X(V),x′} only when the fibre points lie on different connected components.

Here G = ∏_{x∈T} GL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), and when T ≠ ∅ several fibre points lie on the same component. Let C be the component through x′ and H its stabiliser in G. H contains S = ∏ SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), which acts through det-trivial elements and so fixes each geometric component. H also contains the inertia group I(x′/x). The fibre points on C are H·x′, and under the paper's residue-field assumption the decomposition group equals I. So C contains |H|/|I| of them. That number is greater than 1 because S is nonabelian (SL_2(F_ℓ) is nonabelian for every ℓ, including SL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3) while I is abelian ([42, VI.5]). The semilocal ring of C at these points is a normal domain, so it is not the product of its localisations.

Worse, O_{X(V),x′} is then not finite over O_{X,x}. It contains inverses of functions that vanish at another point x″ over x, so it is not inside the integral closure of O_{X,x} in K(C), which is that semilocal ring. So the claim "O_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over O_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" is false as written. A toy model with the same shape: t = s^2 at t = 1 over a field of characteristic ≠ 2 (a Z/2 cover). Here k[s] localised at (s−1) contains 1/(s+1), which is not integral over k[t]_{(t−1)}, and the semilocal ring at {±1} is a domain, not a product.

Lemma 3.27(1) is still true, and the standard completion/henselisation argument plus faithfully flat descent proves it. So the text asserts the key step with an invalid justification, and the descent step is missing. That is a gap, with no effect on any result. It is unrelated to the 47 bracket errors. The same text appears in arXiv v1 and v2 and in the published version. Defence attempted: nothing in the paper's conventions rescues the Zariski reading. Lemma 3.28 explicitly writes 𝒪^∧_{X,x} for completions, so 𝒪_{X,x} and 𝒪_{X_V,x′} mean Zariski local rings. The stalk 𝓛_{σ,x} is also a Zariski stalk ("its stalks at points of X − Y are free"). Taken literally, the displayed equality is false. (f_*𝒪_{X(V)})_x = 𝒪(X(V)) ⊗ 𝒪_{X,x} is the semilocal ring of X(V) along f^{-1}(x). Because X(V) is normal, it is a product of normal domains, one for each irreducible component through the fibre. In this setting a component C has several points over x. G acts transitively on the fibre, and the stabiliser of x′ is I(x′/x) (the residue fields agree), which is cyclic of order e prime to p (cusp inertia). The stabiliser of C contains a copy of SL_2(Z/x^{c_x/2}), whose order is much larger than e. So the semilocal ring has a domain factor with at least two maximal ideals, and it is not ⊕_{x′} 𝒪_{X(V),x′}. The claim "𝒪_{X(V),x′,χ} is free over 𝒪_{X,x}, being a summand of a free module" also fails. 𝒪_{X(V),x′} is not a summand of the stalk and is not finitely generated. If it were free it would have finite rank, hence be integral over 𝒪_{X,x}. But it contains 1/s for some s in the maximal ideal of another point x″ of C over x, and 1/s is not integral. A one-dimensional analogue: Z[i]_{(2+i)} is not free over Z_{(5)}. For the same reason the intermediate map 𝓛_{σ,x} → (𝒪_{X(V),x′} ⊗ W_σ)^{I(x′/x)} cannot be an isomorphism of Zariski stalks, because the right side is not finitely generated. After completion (or henselisation) every step is correct, and freeness descends, so Lemma 3.27(1) is true. Kind is borderline gap/error: the conclusion is right and the repair is standard, but the argument as printed is not valid. Later uses: the proof of 3.27(2) ("the proof of the previous part shows that (𝓛_σ)_A ≅ (f_*(𝒪_{X(V)_A} ⊗ W_σ))^G"); p. 347 (X(V)_A/G ≅ X_A "by applying the argument of the proof of Lemma 3.27(1)"); and Lemma 3.28, pp. 348–349 ("as in the proof of Lemma 3.27", "(𝓛^sub_{σ*})^∧_x by the proof of Lemma 3.27(1)"). All of these are formal-local statements, and the corrected completed version supports them. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 341: "In this case, minimal modular lifts of ρ̄ will appear in the σ* := Hom(σ, O)-isotypical part of H^0(X_V, ω))." p. 343: "H^0(X_U, ω^{⊗n} ⊗_{O_X} L_σ) ≅ (H^0(X_V, ω^{⊗n}) ⊗_O W_σ)^G = Hom_{O[G]}(W_σ^*, H^0(X_V, ω^{⊗n})) … The sheaf L_σ will thus allow us to extract the W_σ^*-part of the space of modular forms at level V." p. 350: "Let T_∅ denote the ring of Hecke operators acting on H_0(X_U, ω ⊗ L_σ) generated by Hecke operators away from S(ρ̄) ∪ {p}. … Theorem 3.30 The map φ : R^min ↠ T_{∅,m∅} is an isomorphism and T_{∅,m∅} acts freely on H_0(X_U, ω ⊗ L_σ)_{m∅}." p. 351, step (3): "H_i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ L_σ) = H^i(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (ω^{2−n} ⊗ L^sub_{σ*})_{K/O})^∨. We use this to endow the left hand side with a Hecke action." p. 353, step (4): "let T denote the subalgebra of endomorphisms of H^0(X_{U_1(Q)}, (ω ⊗ L_σ)_{K/O}) … Then there is a Galois representation ρ_Q : G_Q → GL_2(T_m) deforming ρ̄ … minimal outside Q." p. 354: "However, this is precisely the point of the representation W_σ: it cuts out the automorphic representations giving rise to minimal deformations of ρ̄ at the primes in T(ρ̄) (see [15, Lemma 5.1.1])." and "Theorem 1.4 follows from the previous result and Verdier duality as in Sect. 3.8."
sourceIssues.correction:
Theorem 3.30 should concern the module whose Hecke algebra step (4) controls. The paper's convention (p. 341, p. 343, step (4)) is that minimal lifts lie in the W_σ^*-part H^0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ). Accordingly, state Theorem 3.30 in one of two equivalent forms.
(a) Use H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_{σ^*}) in place of H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ). This is the Pontryagin dual of H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L^sub_σ)_{K/O}), which by step (2) agrees with H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O}) at m_∅. Steps (1)–(3) go through with σ and σ^* swapped, and step (4) then supplies R_Q ↠ T_Q verbatim.
(b) Equivalently, keep L_σ but localise at m_∅^* (T_x ↦ tr ρ̄(Frob_x)/det ρ̄(Frob_x), ⟨a⟩ ↦ det ρ̄(a)^{-1}), with R^min(ρ̄^∨) ≅ R^min(ρ̄).
Theorem 1.4 for H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ)_m then follows from (b). Verdier duality D: H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) ≅ H^1(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) matches T_x and ⟨a⟩ on H^1 with ⟨x^{-1}⟩T_x and ⟨a^{-1}⟩ on H_0 (by T_x^t = ⟨x^{-1}⟩T_x, p. 352), so it carries the m_∅^*-part to the m_∅-part. This twisted duality replaces the w_ζ^*-equivariant isomorphism of Sect. 3.8 cited on p. 354. The closing rank-one remark needs the same change. When det ρ̄|I_x = 1 for every x ∈ T(ρ̄), σ ≅ σ^* and the printed statement is correct. The candidate's correction is right in substance. Its alternative branch (that CDT's σ_x is normalised the other way) does not arise; see reason.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this from the printed definitions. (i) By the definition of H_i in §3.2.4 and step (3), H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) is the Pontryagin dual of H^0(X_U, (ω⊗L^sub_{σ*})_{K/O}), with the dual Hecke action. By Lemma 3.27(2), that module is (H^0(X_V, ω(−∞))_{K/O} ⊗ W_{σ*})^G = Hom_G(W_σ, ·). So T_∅ in Theorem 3.30 is the Hecke algebra of the W_σ-part. (ii) Pp. 341 and 343 and step (4) say the minimal lifts of ρ̄ live in H^0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) = Hom_G(W_σ^*, ·), and step (4) builds minimal Galois representations only on that algebra. The patching in Thm 3.26 needs R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} for the algebra acting on H_N = H_0(X_{Δ_N}(Q_N), ω⊗L_σ)_m, which is the σ*-coefficient algebra. Step (4) does not supply this map. (iii) The two parts are genuinely different. dim Hom_G(W, π) = dim Hom_G(W*, π^∨), so they carry contragredient inertial types, and W_σ, W_σ* have mutually inverse central characters on the centre of GL_2(F_x). Take ρ̄|I_x = ξ⊕ξ^x. The two parts can both contain lifts of ρ̄ only if ξ^{-1}⊕ξ^{-x} ≅ ξ⊕ξ^x, i.e. ξ^{1+x} = det ρ̄|I_x = 1. (iv) A concrete case. Let p = 3, x = 5, K = Q(√−2): 5 is inert, 3 splits, class number 1. Take a finite-order Hecke character θ of conductor 5·𝔮, where 11 = 𝔮𝔮̄. Let θ_5 have order 8 on F_25^× and θ_𝔮 be quadratic, so θ(−1) = (−1)(−1) = 1. Then ρ = Ind θ is an odd weight-one Artin representation unramified at 3. Its reduction ρ̄ is irreducible, and 5 is a vexing prime with ξ of order 8. A computation over the order-24 cyclic group gives the type exponents {3,15} against the dual {9,21}, and det ρ̄|I_5 of order 4. ρ itself satisfies Definition 3.1, so R^min has an O-point. Under the paper's convention, the W_σ-part has no characteristic-0 eigenforms at m∅. The x-component of the nebentypus even rules them out mod p, since ω_σ ≢ ω_σ^{-1} (order 4). So T_{∅,m∅} is zero or torsion, and 'R^min ≅ T_{∅,m∅}' fails. (v) The reverse normalisation of [15] is the only way out, and it makes the p. 341 statement and the minimality claim of step (4) false instead. So the paper as printed contains a genuine σ/σ* inconsistency either way. I could not obtain [15] to fix which side, so I report the reading under the paper's own stated convention. Theorem 1.4 is existential in L_σ and survives after the repair. 1. What acts on H_0 (defence fails). By the paper's own definition, H_0(X_U, ω⊗L_σ) = H^0(X_U,(ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_{K/O})^∨, with the dual Hecke action (p. 351; §3.2.4). By Lemma 3.27(2), (H^0(X_V,ω(−∞))⊗W_{σ^*})^G = Hom_G(W_σ, S_1(V)). So T_∅ is the Hecke algebra of the W_σ-part. Step (3) says this itself: 'dim H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L^sub_{σ^*})_m = dim H^0(…,ω⊗L_{σ^*})_m'.
2. Where the Galois representations are built. Step (4) builds them only on the Hecke algebra of H^0(X_{U_1(Q)},(ω⊗L_σ)_{K/O}) = Hom_G(W_σ^*, ·), the W_σ^*-part. So the 'same proof as Theorem 3.26' has no map R_{Q_N} ↠ T_{Q_N,m} for the patched modules H_0(…,ω⊗L_σ)_m, and no φ for T_∅. Nothing nearby bridges the two parts:
- the contragredient in step (3) sends the W_σ^*-part at m to the W_σ-part at m*, not m;
- the 'self-dual up to twist' remark in v1 changes ρ̄ to a twist of ρ̄.
3. Which side is right: I checked [15] (CDT, Taylor's copy).
- In §5.1, σ_{S,p} = Θ(χ_p), with ρ̄|I_p ≅ χ̄_p∘η_{p,2} ⊕ χ̄_p∘Frob∘η_{p,2}.
- Lemma 5.1.1: π ∈ N_S iff Hom_{U_S}(σ_S, π^∞) ≠ 0.
- CDT's Notation fixes η_1 = ε^{-1}, with the arithmetic-Frobenius normalisation.
- Θ(χ) has central character χ|Z_x^×.
Now take a minimal lift f. Then det ρ_f|I_x = χ|Z_x^× ∘ ε^{-1}, so the x-part of the nebentypus of f is (χ|Z_x^×)^{-1}. That character is how scalars of G act under the moduli action α ↦ α∘g. It is the central character of σ_x^*. So under the paper's moduli action, minimal forms lie in the W_σ^*-part: p. 341 and step (4) are right, and the statement of Theorem 3.30 is the slip.
4. The two parts really differ. Hom_G(W_σ, π) ≅ Hom_G(W_σ^*, π^∨), and CDT Lemmas 3.2.1(2) and 4.2.4(3) apply. Together they show the W_σ-part contains only forms of the dual type, whose reduction is ξ^{-1}⊕ξ^{-x}. That is ≇ ξ⊕ξ^x unless det ρ̄|I_x = ξ^{1+x} = 1.
- Example: p = 3, x = 5, ξ of order 8 on F_25^×; then ξ^5 ≠ ξ and ξ^6 ≠ 1.
- A dihedral ρ̄ = Ind_K ψ is one realisation.
In such a case H_0(X_U, ω_K⊗L_σ)_{m_∅} = 0 (in fact T_{∅,m_∅} = 0, by step (4)'s Hasse-invariant argument). But R^min ≠ 0, and it has a characteristic-zero point when there is a minimal weight-one lift. So Theorem 3.30 as printed is false.
5. What uses it. Theorem 3.30 is used only to deduce Theorem 1.4 (p. 354), and Corollaries 1.5 and 1.6 come from Theorem 1.4. Theorem 1.4 is existential in the bundle and still holds for L_σ via form (b). So the stated result that fails is Theorem 3.30 (and the rank-one remark); Theorem 1.4 and its corollaries are unaffected.
Confidence: the σ/σ^* mismatch is certain. The direction (the statement is wrong, not step (4)) rests on the normalisation check in point 3.

The text and page images show Remark 3.4, Lemma 3.5, Lemma 3.6, Lemma 3.7, Proposition 3.8, Assumption 3.9 and Remark 3.10, so no Proposition 3.7 exists. PDF pages 25–26 (pp. 321–322) print "Lemma 3.7 Let Δ be a quotient of Δ_Q. Then: … (2) For i = 0, 1, we have an isomorphism H^i(X_Δ(Q), ω(−∞)_{K/O})_m → H^i(X_Δ(Q), ω_{K/O})_m". Its argument is the same: take the exact sequence through the cusps and use the Eisenstein property from Remark 3.4. So the number 3.7(2) is correct and only the label "Proposition" is wrong. The arXiv v2 has the same wording (cg-v2.txt line 2104: "(2) (Proposition 3.7 (2))") while also printing "Lemma 3.7." (line 949). This is a wrong environment label and has nothing to do with the 47 known bracket errors. It does not affect the mathematics, because a reader can find the result from the number alone and nothing later depends on the label.

sourceIssues.locator: §3.9.2 (the proof of Theorem 1.4 with vexing primes), proof of Theorem 3.30, item (2) (the analogue of Lemma 3.7(2), which the paper labels "Proposition 3.7 (2)"), published p. 351 (PDF p. 55). The claim rests on Remark 3.4, p. 316 (PDF p. 20), which makes the same kind of transitivity claim for (Z/NQZ)^× on C_Δ(Q). The text is identical in arXiv v2 (p. 40 for §3.9.2; Remark 3.4 at v2 line 732). arXiv v1 has neither transitivity claim: its Lemma 3.7(2) proof just says "the action of Hecke on H^0(X, I) is Eisenstein".
sourceIssues.printed: (2) (Proposition 3.7 (2)): ... and it suffices to show that the cohomology of the last term (which is concentrated in degree 0) is Eisenstein. However, the argument of Remark 3.4 (noting that the group ∏_{x∈T(ρ̄)} GL_2(Z_x) × ∏_{x∈P(ρ̄)} Z_x^× acts transitively on the set of cusps in X_{V_Δ(Q)}) shows that H^0(X_{U_Δ(Q)}, (f_*((ω ⊗ W_σ)|_{C_{V_Δ(Q)}}))^G) = (H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) ⊗_O W_σ)^G is Eisenstein, which gives the desired result.   [Remark 3.4, p. 316, which this relies on: "... but note that the group (Z/NQZ)^× acts transitively on the set of cusps in C_Δ(Q). In particular, suppose f ∈ H^0(C_Δ(Q), ω_k^{⊗n}) is a non-zero mod p eigenform ... Then f cannot vanish at any cusp and the formula [28, (3.5)] implies that ... T_x(f) = (1 + χ(x)x^{n−1})f."]
sourceIssues.correction: Delete the parenthetical transitivity claim, because it is false. Justify the Eisenstein property type by type. The cusps of X_{V_Δ(Q)} have local "types" at each prime x of Q, of P(ρ̄), of S(ρ̄)−(T∪P) and at the auxiliary Γ_1(q) prime. These are the N(Z_x)\GL_2(Z_x)/U_0-type double cosets, i.e. the analogues of '∞' and '0'. The listed group, even with all the diamond operators added, preserves every type; within a type it permutes the cusps. On H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω^n), each T_x (x ∉ S∪Q∪{p}) acts as B_x + x^{n−1}A_x. Here A_x and B_x come from left translation by diag(x^{-1},1) and diag(1,x^{-1}) away from x. They permute the cusps and rescale by roots of unity, they commute, and they are multiplicative in x. So every simultaneous eigenvalue has the form ψ_1(x)+x^{n−1}ψ_2(x) with ψ_i finite-order characters, and the associated semisimple Galois representation ψ_1 ⊕ ψ_2ε^{n−1} is reducible. T_x commutes with G and acts trivially on W_σ, so the submodule (H^0(C_{V_Δ(Q)}, ω) ⊗ W_σ)^G is also Eisenstein. The conclusion of item (2) is therefore correct. The candidate's first proposed fix is right and is the minimal one. Its Atkin–Lehner alternative is only a sketch: at P and S−(T∪P) the Atkin–Lehner element conjugates V_x to a different group, so it needs more care.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 351 and p. 316 and transcribed the text. The claim is refuted by an equivariant projection. Here V_Δ(Q) = ∏_{x∉Q} V_x × ∏_{x∈Q} (a group between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}), and patching needs Q ≠ ∅. Fix x ∈ Q and let W' = ∏_{y≠x} GL_2(Z_y) × U_{0,x}. Then W' contains V_Δ(Q), and it also contains the group K' = ∏_{T} GL_2(Z_y) × ∏_{P} Z_y^×, whose components all lie at primes other than x. The projection X_{V_Δ(Q)} → X_{W'} = X_0(x) is therefore K'-equivariant. K' acts trivially on X_0(x) because it lies inside W': on cusps, [h]_V ↦ [hg]_V maps to [hg]_{W'} = [h]_{W'}. The projection is surjective on cusps, and X_0(x) has two cusps, 0 and ∞. So K' has at least two orbits on the cusps of X_{V_Δ(Q)}. Equivalently, the local Bruhat type in B(Q_x)\GL_2(Q_x)/U_{0,x}, which has 2 elements, is an invariant that K' preserves. The same happens even when Q = ∅, at primes in S − (T∪P) with U_1(x^{c_x}) level.

Remark 3.4 fails in the same way. The diamond operators commute with X_Δ(Q) → X_0(NQ), which has at least 2 cusps when NQ > 1. Its consequence is also false: a Hecke eigenvector can vanish at the ∞-type cusps and have eigenvalue ψ_1(x) + ψ_2(x)x^{n−1} ≠ 1 + χ(x)x^{n−1}. An example is the constant-term vector of E_n^{χ,1} for n ≥ 3 and nontrivial χ.

The target conclusion (the boundary term is Eisenstein) is still true by the standard constant-term argument. So a false assertion is used as a proof step, while the result survives. arXiv v1 simply asserted the Eisenstein property without this faulty justification. Defence attempts. (a) Could "cusps in X_{V_Δ(Q)}" mean only the cusps over a fixed cusp of X_{U_Δ(Q)}? G acts transitively on those fibres, but then the factor ∏_P Z_x^× would be pointless, and the text says "the set of cusps". Also the argument of Remark 3.4 needs a global statement: an eigenvector is non-zero at '∞', and its eigenvalue is read off there. (b) Could "cusps" mean Galois orbits? Galois acts through det, i.e. by upper-triangular matrices, which preserve the types. Neither reading rescues the claim.

Why it is false. Adelically, cusps = B(Q)\GL_2(A^∞)/V = ({±1}^2·N(Ẑ))\∏_x GL_2(Z_x)/V_x. The listed group acts only on the T- and P-components on the right. At x ∈ Q, where V_x lies between U_{1,x} and U_{0,x}, the invariant N(Z_x)\GL_2(Z_x)/U_{0,x} = N\P^1(F_x) has two values. Neither the global ±1 nor the group can change it. At x ∈ P, the Z_x^× action is by elements of U_0(x^{c_x}), which preserve the c_x+1 ≥ 2 valuation types.

Brute-force check (script work/agents/vK4-9B/cusps57.py): p=3, vexing t=5 (5≡−1 mod 3, V_t=Γ(5)), Q={7} (7≡1 mod 3) with U_{1,7}-level. There are 288 cusps. GL_2(Z/5) has 6 orbits on them, and adding the diamonds at 7 still leaves 2 orbits.

So the claim fails whenever Q≠∅, P≠∅, S≠T, or the auxiliary Γ_1(q) level is used. It holds only in the degenerate case S=T, Q=∅ with no auxiliary level, which footnote 4 says needs that level anyway. Patching uses #Q_N = q ≥ 1, so the claim is false exactly where it is used.

Nuance on the candidate's reason: its example has T=∅, but §3.9.2 assumes T≠∅. The failure persists with T≠∅, as above.

Consequences. Item (2) is used in item (3): "which in turn, by point (2) above, is equal to". Through that it feeds the analogue of Prop 3.8 and the patching proof of Thm 3.30, and hence Thm 1.4. The conclusion of item (2) is true by the standard type-by-type computation, so no stated result changes. Only the given justification fails, so 'affects' is 'the proof'.

I redid the computation with n = 1, the case in use here: the left-hand side is ω ⊗ L_σ. Write c(r) = ΨrΨ^{−1} for an operator r on H^0. The printed relations then give c(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x) = T_x and c(⟨a⟩) = ⟨a^{−1}⟩. It follows that c(T_x) = c(⟨x⟩)c(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x) = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x on H_1. So Ψ(H^0_{m*}) = H_{1,m} exactly when β(r) = α(c(r)), which gives β(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x). The printed β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a^{−1}⟩) and β(U_y^t) = α(U_y) agree with this computation. Only β(T_x) has the wrong sign in the exponent.

The paper's own final step gives an independent check that does not depend on how ⟨a⟩ is normalised. The proof says that taking contragredients swaps H^0(ω⊗L_σ)_{m*} and H^0(ω⊗L_{σ*})_m, so m* has to be the contragredient of m. Item (4) on p. 353 uses the Hecke polynomial X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. With that convention, the contragredient of an eigensystem (t_x, d(a)) is (t_x·d(x)^{−1}, d(a)^{−1}). That again gives β(T_x) = α(T_x)α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}. With the printed β, the contragredient of m* would have T_x-eigenvalue α(⟨x⟩)^2α(T_x), which is not m.

The discrepancy is real in general. α(⟨x⟩) is the reduction of the nebentypus, which is det ρ̄(Frob_x) in weight 1, and it has order > 2 in general. So α(⟨x⟩)^2 is not identically 1, and read literally, the printed m* makes both the step "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" and the contragredient step false.

The error is in β, not in T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x: the Ψ relations and the contragredient check both force the corrected β. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it.

Scope: m* and β appear only in this item, and nothing later uses the formula. With the obvious fix, the argument goes through exactly as the authors intend, so no stated result is affected. As the candidate noted, I did not check the scalar normalisation of T_x^t from [31]. It would only change x-power factors, which are trivial when n = 1.

A separate small slip that is not part of this item: the display at the foot of p. 352 has "ω^n ⊗ L_σ" where n = 1 is meant. Defence attempted and it fails. Two independent checks both force the corrected β.

(1) The paper's own relations with n = 1, the case in use. Take v in H^0(ω⊗L_σ) with T_x v = τv and ⟨x⟩v = δv, and put w = Ψ(v). Then T_x w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x v) = δ^{−1}τ w and ⟨x⟩w = Ψ(⟨x^{−1}⟩v) = δ^{−1}w. For w to lie in the m-part we need δ^{−1} ≡ α(⟨x⟩) and δ^{−1}τ ≡ α(T_x). So τ ≡ α(⟨x⟩)^{−1}α(T_x) = α(⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x). The same computation gives β(⟨a⟩) = α(⟨a⟩)^{−1} and β(U_y^t) = α(U_y), exactly as printed. So only β(T_x) is off, by a factor α(⟨x⟩)^2.

The printed β cannot be rescued by reading T_x^t = ⟨x^{−1}⟩T_x differently. That formula follows from the paper's own isogeny argument (φ^t : (E,α) → (E', x∘α')) with the moduli convention ⟨a⟩f(E,α) = f(E,aα). It also agrees with v1, which has D(T_x c) = ⟨x⟩^{−1}T_x D(c).

(2) The paper's final step, which does not depend on Ψ. The proof says that taking contragredients swaps H^0(ω⊗L_σ)_{m*}⊗C and H^0(ω⊗L_{σ*})_m⊗C, so m* must be the contragredient eigensystem of m. The paper's convention (p. 326) is that m_∅ is generated by ϖ, T_x − tr ρ̄(Frob_x) and ⟨x⟩ − det ρ̄(Frob_x); item (4) likewise uses X^2 − T_xX + ⟨x⟩. Since ρ̄^∨ ≅ ρ̄ ⊗ det^{−1}, the contragredient has T_x ↦ t_x/d_x and ⟨a⟩ ↦ d_a^{−1}, where d = det ρ̄(Frob). This is again the corrected β. The printed m* would instead need a residual representation with trace d_x t_x and determinant d_x^{−1}. Its trace is that of ρ̄⊗det ρ̄, whose determinant is d^3, so this is impossible unless (det ρ̄)^4 = 1. The printed and corrected ideals differ as soon as d_x^2 ≠ 1 and t_x ≠ 0 for some x, which happens in general, since det ρ̄ can have order > 2. Read literally, then, the claim "RHS = dim H^0(...)_{m*}" is false and the contragredient step fails.

Why this is a misprint and not an error. It is a single inverted exponent. The correct value follows at once from the displayed relations just above it. The earlier version (v1) states the correct ideal, and the argument goes through verbatim with it.

Consequences. m* and β occur only in this item; the other m* on pp. 417 ff. and in §9 are unrelated. The item proves that H_0(X_Δ(Q), ω⊗L_σ)_m is balanced, which is then used in patching for Theorem 3.30, i.e. Theorem 1.4 with vexing primes. With the fix, that conclusion stands, so no stated result is affected. The mathematics is right as intended, so under PROTOCOL §18 'affects' is 'nothing'. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors, and the 2022 Correction does not cover it. A separate cosmetic slip: the display "dim_K H^0(X_{U_0(Q)}, ω^n ⊗ L_σ)_{m*}" has ω^n where n = 1 is meant.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered page image (PDF p. 57 = p. 353, §3.9.2, proof of Theorem 3.30, item (4)). The text is exactly as quoted. The accepted arXiv version 1207.4224v2 has the same wording, so this is not one of the 47 bracket errors. By the paper's own conventions the printed statement is wrong:
(i) Item (4) is "the analogue of" Theorem 3.11. That theorem says ρ_Q is unramified outside NQ, i.e. outside S(ρ̄) ∪ Q, which includes being unramified at p. The printed version swaps Q for {p}. It permits ramification at p, which is exactly what Theorem 3.11 rules out ("Theorem 3.11 is showing that the Galois representation is unramified at p", p. 327). It also claims ρ_Q is unramified at every x ∈ Q.
(ii) It contradicts the next sentence. η is the square root of ν = det ρ̄ · det(ρ_Q)^{-1}, which is "unramified outside Q". The paper then says ρ'_Q = ρ_Q ⊗ η is minimal outside Q. By Definition 3.1(2), that requires ρ'_Q to be unramified at every x ∉ Q ∪ S(ρ̄), p included. So ρ_Q must be unramified at p. On the other hand, ramification at Q is exactly what "minimal outside Q" allows. T_m is built from H^0(X_{U_1(Q)}, ...), on which the diamond operators at x ∈ Q act, and these give the ramification at Q used in patching.
(iii) The trace condition is ill-posed at Q. p. 345 (PDF p. 49) says that on X_{U_i(Q)} the operators are T_x for x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ Q ∪ {p}, and U_y for y ∈ Q. Item (4) itself defines T using "T_x, U_y and ⟨a⟩" and m using U_x − α_x for x ∈ Q. So "trace T_x for all x ∉ S(ρ̄) ∪ {p}" refers to operators T_x (x ∈ Q) that are not defined in T, and to Frob_x at primes where ρ_Q may ramify.
The proof that follows establishes the corrected statement: it constructs ρ_Q so that ρ'_Q satisfies the conditions of Definition 3.1, using Sections 3.3–3.7, the unramified-at-p argument. The error is a slip in writing the analogue's statement, not a mathematical gap. The proposed correction is right.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.1, Lemma 4.2 ('Moreover…') and its proof, p. 355 (same in arXiv v2, §4.1)
sourceIssues.printed: p. 355 (PDF p. 59), §4.1: "Lemma 4.2 If B is a complete local Cohen–Macaulay O-algebra and admits a dualizing module ω_B with μ generators, then the same is true for the power series ring A = B[T1, . . . , Tn]. Moreover, the same is also true for B⊗̂_O C, for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection. Proof For power series rings this is a special case of the discussion above. Consider now the case of B⊗̂_O C. By assumption, C is a quotient of O[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence. Hence B⊗̂_O C is a quotient of B[T1, . . . , Tn] by a regular sequence, and the result follows from the discussion above applied to the maps B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B and B[T1, . . . , Tn] → B⊗̂_O C respectively." The single brackets are among the 47 known bracket errors and should read ⟦T1,…,Tn⟧; arXiv v2 prints B[[T1,…,Tn]] and O[[T1,…,Tn]].
sourceIssues.correction:
Add a Tor-independence hypothesis, for example: "…for any complete local O-algebra C which is a complete intersection, provided that B or C is flat over O." Over the DVR O, this is equivalent to Tor_1^O(B,C) = 0, which is exactly the condition the proof needs.

If B is O-flat: (ϖ, T1, …, Tn) is a regular sequence on B⟦T⟧, so Tor_1^{O⟦T⟧}(k, B⟦T⟧) = 0. By the local flatness criterion, B⟦T⟧ is then flat over O⟦T⟧.

If C is O-flat: write B = O⟦S⟧/I. Then Tor_i^{O⟦S,T⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B⟦T⟧) = Tor_i^{O⟦S⟧}(C⟦S⟧, B). This is 0 for i > 0, because C⟦S⟧ is O⟦S⟧-flat by the same criterion.

In either case, a regular sequence f in O⟦T⟧ with C = O⟦T⟧/(f) stays regular on B⟦T⟧, and B⟦T⟧/(f) = B⊗̂_O C, so the printed proof then works. "B or C" is better than "B O-flat" alone, because it also covers the remark after the lemma (B⟦Δ⟧ for arbitrary B, where C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat).
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the counterexample independently. The paper's conventions allow it: C_O is "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k" and nothing requires flatness. The proof also defines "complete intersection" only as "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence".

Take B = k = O/ϖ. It is complete local, Cohen–Macaulay of dimension 0, with ω_B = k, so μ = 1. Take C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ).
- In the regular local ring O⟦x,y,z⟧ with maximal ideal (ϖ,x,y,z), xy−ϖ lies in m but not in m². So R = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is regular of dimension 3, hence a domain.
- In R, xz−ϖ = x(z−y). Both factors are nonzero, as their images in k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy) show. So xz−ϖ is a nonzerodivisor, and C is a complete intersection of dimension 2.
- B⊗̂_O C = C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) = k⟦x,y,z⟧/((x)∩(y,z)). Its associated primes are (x) and (y,z), with dim R/(y,z) = 1. Since depth ≤ dim R/p for every associated prime p, the depth is 1 while the dimension is 2. So the ring is not Cohen–Macaulay.
- The proof breaks exactly at "quotient of B⟦T⟧ by a regular sequence": in k⟦x,y,z⟧, xz times y lies in (xy), but y does not. So xz is a zero-divisor mod xy.
- Necessarily C here is not O-flat: ϖ = xy lies in the minimal prime (x) of C.

The second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is therefore false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint.

Downstream effect: Lemma 4.2 is cited only in §4.1 (pp. 363–364).
- For R_loc⟦x1,…,xn⟧, B = R̃†, which the proof of Thm 4.3 states is O-flat.
- For T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧, B = T_{1,m} is O-flat and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The B⟦Δ⟧ remark holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat. The candidate's line that "every application has B O-flat" is slightly wrong for this remark, where B is arbitrary. The remark is still true through the C-flat variant.

The paper also says §4.1 is "not needed for our main results". Beyond what the candidate addressed, the R_loc application also needs C = ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a complete intersection. That implicitly uses the R_v being O-flat, which I did not check further. So the flaw is in a stated result, Lemma 4.2, and the paper's conclusions stay intact. DEFENCE ATTEMPTS, all of which fail.
(a) No flatness convention. The Notation section (p. 305) defines C_O as "complete Noetherian local O-algebras with residue field k", with no flatness. §4.1 adds none. B = k and B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx) are allowed.
(b) "Complete intersection" cannot be read as "O-flat relative CI". The paper uses the term in the absolute sense for non-flat rings: Thm 1.3 (p. 302) and p. 380 say "If dim(T_m)=0, then T_m is a complete intersection", and there T_m is Artinian. The proof's own gloss, "a quotient of O⟦T1,…,Tn⟧ by a regular sequence", is satisfied by the counterexamples below.
(c) No nearby statement supplies the missing Tor-vanishing.

COUNTEREXAMPLES (checked by hand).
1. X-K4-14: B = O⟦x⟧/(ϖx).
- B is a hypersurface of dimension 1, hence CM and Gorenstein (ω_B = B, μ = 1). It is CM because ϖ+x lies in neither associated prime (ϖ), (x).
- C = O⟦y⟧/(ϖy) is a CI.
- B⊗̂_O C = O⟦x,y⟧/(ϖx,ϖy) = O⟦x,y⟧/((ϖ)∩(x,y)). Its minimal primes have coheights 2 and 1, so it is not equidimensional and not CM.
- The step that fails: ϖy·x = 0 in B⟦y⟧ with x ≠ 0.
2. H-part1b-1 / X-K5-0: B = k (CM, ω = k, μ = 1) and C = O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ, xz−ϖ), or (xy−ϖ, xz).
- xy−ϖ ∉ m², so O⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy−ϖ) is a regular domain, and x(z−y) and xz are nonzero in it. So C is a CI of dimension 2.
- C/ϖC = k⟦x,y,z⟧/(xy,xz) has associated primes (x) and (y,z).
- It has depth 1: y+x is regular, and modulo it x ≠ 0 is killed by m. Its dimension is 2, so it is not CM.
In all of these, neither B nor C is O-flat. As shown in the correction, flatness of either one is enough.

CONSEQUENCES. Lemma 4.2 is cited only on pp. 365–366.
- (i) R_loc⟦x⟧ = R̃† ⊗̂ (⊗̂_v R_v)⟦x⟧, with B = R̃†. The proof of Thm 4.3 (p. 356) says it is O-flat.
- (ii) T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O⟦Φ⟧. Here B = T_{1,m} is O-flat because the forms are ϖ-torsion free, and C = O⟦Φ⟧ is O-flat.
- The remark after the lemma, "B⟦Δ⟧ for any B", holds because C = O⟦Δ⟧ is O-flat.
So the multiplicity-two conclusion survives with the corrected lemma. Also, §4.1 is "not needed for our main results" (p. 355).

A side point that is independent of this candidate: application (i) also needs ⊗̂_v R_v⟦x⟧ to be a CI, which implicitly uses O-flatness of the R_v. The R_v are O⟦Δ⟧-power-series rings or O⟦x1..x4⟧/(r) with r = C(T)−T; I did not check further whether ϖ ∤ r.

Verdict: the second assertion of Lemma 4.2 is false as printed. It is not a bracket misprint, and the 2022 Correction does not fix it. v1 and v2 have the same text.

sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. We have  H_{R/x}(t)/(1 − t) ≥ H_R(t) · (1 − t^d)/(1 − t),  and equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. Moreover, if there is an isomorphism  R ≃ gr(R) = ⊕ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1},  and x is pure of degree d, then equality holds if and only if x is a regular element.   [Remark after the proof, pp. 357–358: "Note that, in the non-graded case, the converse is not true, namely, x may be regular of degree one and yet the equality H_{R/x}(t) = H_R(t)(1−t) fails; as an example one may take R = k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] and x = φ^6. Then x is regular, but (1+2t+2t^2+t^3)/(1−t) > (1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5)/(1−t) = H_R(t)." Here k[...] is one of the known bracket errors and should be k⟦φ^6, φ^7, φ^15⟧.]
sourceIssues.correction: Minimal fix: in the first sentence, replace "equality holds if and only if x is a regular element" with "equality holds only if x is a regular element" (equivalently: if x is a zero-divisor, the inequality is strict). Keep "if and only if" only in the 'Moreover' clause, where R ≃ gr(R), meaning R is the completion of its associated graded ring, and x is pure of degree d. A true 'iff' also holds in the ungraded case if "x is regular" is replaced by "the degree-d initial form of x is a regular element of gr(R)". That is not what the paper intends, though: its remark uses "regular" to mean regular in R.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered PDF pages 61–62 (pp. 357–358). The first sentence of the statement really does say "equality holds if and only if x is a regular element", with no graded hypothesis. The setup on p. 356 is just "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k". The authors' remark right after the proof ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true") gives a counterexample to that first sentence.

I redid the computation myself with a Python script over the semigroup ⟨6,7,15⟩, using the m-adic order of φ^s = the maximal number of generators summing to s.
- H_R = 1+3t+4t^2+5t^3+5t^4+6t^5+6t^6+…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors: the only bracket error nearby is k[φ^6, φ^7, φ^15] in the remark, which is already known. Defence attempted and failed. The setup on p. 356 is only "a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪) with residue field k", with no grading. "Regular element" gets no special definition. The paper's own remark refutes exactly that ("in the non-graded case, the converse is not true").

- H_R has coefficients 1,3,4,5,5,6,6,…, so (1−t)H_R = 1+2t+t^2+t^3+t^5.

The proof gives only two things: (a) x not regular ⇒ strict inequality (Krull intersection argument), which is the 'only if' direction and holds in general; and (b) x regular and R ≃ gr(R) ⇒ equality. Consequences: Lemma 4.4 is cited only in the proof of Lemma 4.6 (p. 360). There it is used in two ways:

sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 4.4 Let x ∈ 𝔪^d. We have H_{R/x}(t)/(1 − t) ≥ H_R(t) · (1 − t^d)/(1 − t), and equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. Moreover, if there is an isomorphism  R ≃ gr(R) = ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1},  and x is pure of degree d, then equality holds if and only if x is a regular element. [proof:] "Finally, assume that x is a regular element, and that R ≃ gr(R)." [p. 358:] "All the relations in B are pure of degree two, and hence there is an isomorphism B ≃ gr(B)."
sourceIssues.correction: Read the hypothesis as: R is isomorphic to the 𝔪-adic completion ∏_n 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} of gr(R). In other words, R ≅ k⟦x_1,…,x_r⟧/I with I generated by homogeneous polynomials, and 'pure of degree d' refers to that grading. The same reading applies to 'B ≃ gr(B)' on p. 358.
sourceIssues.reason:
The setup on p. 356 makes R a complete local k-algebra (R, 𝔪). The ring B that the lemma is applied to is a quotient of the power series ring k⟦a,b,c,φ1,φ2,φ3⟧ (printed with single brackets, which is one of the known bracket errors). By Lemma 4.6/4.7, B has Krull dimension 3.

The displayed ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} = k[a,…,φ3]/(homogeneous quadrics) is a finitely generated k-algebra of positive dimension. It therefore has infinitely many maximal ideals, so it is not local and not 𝔪-adically complete, and no ring isomorphism B ≃ ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1} exists. As printed, the hypothesis can only hold for Artinian R, and the claim 'B ≃ gr(B)' is literally false.

The intended meaning is clear, and the paper uses it elsewhere: the proof of Lemma 4.6 begins 'Let R be a complete local Cohen–Macaulay Noetherian graded k-algebra' and then invokes 'Lemma 4.4 (in the graded case)'.

With the completed reading, the proof works. Take R = Ĝ with G standard graded and x ∈ G_d regular. Then R/𝔪^{m+d} = ⨁_{j<m+d} G_j, and x·y ∈ 𝔪^{m+d} forces the components y_j with j < m to vanish. So the kernel is exactly 𝔪^m/𝔪^{m+d}, as the proof claims. B satisfies this reading because its defining relations are homogeneous quadrics. The induction in Lemma 4.6 keeps the reading, since quotients by homogeneous elements stay completions of graded rings.

This is an abuse of notation, not a wrong idea, so it is a misprint that affects nothing. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also separate from the 'if and only if' problem in the first sentence of Lemma 4.4 (candidates X-K5-1 / H-part1b-0). Confidence is medium only because some readers treat 'R ≃ gr(R)' for complete local rings as standard shorthand. The explicit '= ⨁ 𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}' makes the printed statement literally wrong.

sourceIssues.printed: On the other hand, since all the relations are trivial in 𝔪^2, we have dim(𝔪/𝔪^2) = 3. Hence the Hilbert polynomial of C is 1+3t, and the sequence is regular in A.
sourceIssues.correction: "Hence the Hilbert series H_C(t) of C is 1 + 3t"
sourceIssues.reason:
The only notion the paper defines is the Hilbert series H_R(t) = Σ dim_k(𝔪^n/𝔪^{n+1}) t^n (p. 356). Lemma 4.6 is stated in terms of H_{B/I}(t) = 1+3t, and the proof of Lemma 4.7 itself opens with 'it suffices to show that the Hilbert series of B/I … is 1+3t'.

C = B/I is a quotient of k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,xz,yz) with dim 𝔪/𝔪^2 = 3, so C ≅ k⟦x,y,z⟧/(x,y,z)^2. It is Artinian with Hilbert function 1, 3, 0, 0, …. Its Hilbert series is therefore 1+3t, while its Hilbert polynomial in the standard sense (the polynomial agreeing with the Hilbert function for n ≫ 0) is 0.

The word 'polynomial' is a terminology slip for 'series' (the series happens to be a polynomial here). The computation and the comparison with Lemma 4.6 are correct under the intended reading. I also rechecked the relations of C from those of B (a = 0, φ3 = −φ2, φ1 = −(b+c)): they match the printed list, and they give xz = yz = xy = x^2 = y^2 = z^2 = 0. This is not a bracket error.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 361 (PDF p. 65): "One knows that ρ̄ occurs as the mod-p reduction of a modular form of weight 2 and level N*, where N* = N if k = 2 and Np otherwise."
sourceIssues.correction: "N* = N if k(ρ̄) = 2 and Np otherwise": k is the residue field; Serre's weight k(ρ̄) is meant.
sourceIssues.reason:
[Review: re-scoped to the p. 361 slip; the ⟨ρ̄ε⁻¹⟩ misprint this entry first recorded is E83.] The text later says 'Thus N* = pN (since p is odd)', which uses k(ρ̄) = p, so k(ρ̄) is meant; k is the residue field throughout. I checked the page images at 250 dpi, and the printed text is as quoted. The main point is a real misprint. The Notation section on p. 305 defines ⟨χ⟩: G → O^× only for a character χ: G → k^×. But ρ̄ε^{−1} is a 2-dimensional representation, not a character. Elsewhere the authors write the determinant explicitly: "ν := ⟨det ρ̄⟩ det(ρ_{Q,m})^{−1}" on p. 332, and ⟨det(ρ̄)⟩ in §3.4 of arXiv v2. So here the word "det" has been dropped, and it is dropped in both occurrences.

I redid the bookkeeping. For weight-2 forms with nebentypus χ, det ρ = ε·χ, so ε^{−1} det ρ = χ, as the paper says. Reducing, χ ≡ det ρ̄·ε̄^{−1} mod m. So χ = ⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·χ_p, where χ_p is the p-power-order part, a character of Z_p⊗(Z/NpZ)^×. Since p ∤ N, this group is Z_p⊗(Z/NZ)^× = Φ × Z_p⊗∏_{x|N, x∤M}(Z/xZ)^×. On Φ, χ_p = φ; on the other factor, χ_p = ψ. After twisting by ψ^{−1/2}, det = εχψ^{−1} = ε·⟨det ρ̄ ε̄^{−1}⟩·φ. This reduces to det ρ̄, and on G_p it equals εω^{−1} times an unramified character, as the ordinary ring R† of §3.7 needs. So the proposed correction is right.

The other two parts of the candidate are much weaker. "k = 2" is a notation clash with the residue field k, but the meaning k(ρ̄) = 2 is clear: the text later says "Thus N* = pN (since p is odd)", which uses k(ρ̄) = p. "∏_{x∤M}" is shorthand, since χ is a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, so x | Np is implicit. Neither needs its own entry.

Nothing depends on the misprint. The intended meaning is clear from the notation convention and the computation. Neither the statement of Theorem 4.8 nor the proof that follows (Lemma 4.11 uses χ_φ only as the fixed determinant) is affected.

sourceIssues.reason: The candidate's premise holds. At a harmless prime v, ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible, so ρ̄^{I_v} = 0 and the conductor exponent is at least 2. Hence v^2 | N and M is never squarefree when M > 1. Read with x ranging over all divisors of M, the first product is the wrong group: for M = v^2 it gives two copies of the p-part of (Z/vZ)^×. The usual convention that the index x is prime fixes the first formula. Under that convention it equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/MZ)^×, since for x ≠ p the tensor Z_p ⊗ (Z/x^eZ)^× equals Z_p ⊗ (Z/xZ)^×. The second product is genuinely wrong as printed even with x prime. It runs over all primes not dividing M, so it is infinite. It must be cut down to primes x | N (x = p adds nothing because p is odd). Only then is 'the restriction of χ', a character of (Z/NpZ)^×, meaningful. The intended meaning is clear from context, so this is a misprint that affects nothing. Confidence is medium only because the Φ half could be defended as an abuse of notation. The ψ half cannot.

sourceIssues.locator: §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, published p. 363 (PDF p. 67), paragraph beginning "The reason for dealing with the harmless primes". arXiv v2 (p. 49) has the same text. arXiv v1 has the first sentence (the ring isomorphism "up to unramified twists") but not the "Equivalently…" or "The only time…" sentences, and it defines "harmless" differently.
sourceIssues.printed: p. 363 (PDF p. 67), first paragraph, read from the page image: "The reason for dealing with the harmless primes in this manner is as follows. For all non-harmless v ≠ p, the conductor-minimal deformation ring of ρ̄|G_v (which classifies deformations which appear at level Γ_1(N)) is isomorphic to the ring R_{v,φ} (up to unramified twists). Equivalently, for non-harmless primes, any characteristic zero lift ρ of ρ̄ is uniquely twist equivalent to a lift of minimal conductor. The only time this is not true is when v ≡ 1 mod p and ρ̄ has trivial invariants under I_v. Since we are assuming that ρ̄|_{G_v} is minimally ramified amongst all its twists, this only happens when ρ̄|_{G_v} is absolutely irreducible and v ≡ 1 mod p." The next paragraph, which depends on it, reads: "Kisin's improvement of the Taylor–Wiles method yields an isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p]." On p. 362: "(2) When v ≠ p, R_v = R_{v,φ} is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with determinant χ_φ|G_v."
sourceIssues.correction: The exceptional set is wrong. Uniqueness of the minimal-conductor twist, and the claimed isomorphism with R_{v,φ} up to unramified twist, also fail at the non-harmless primes of Lemma 4.11 case (3): v ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄^{I_v} one-dimensional and ρ̄^{ss}|G_v unramified. Take a lift in R_{v,φ} with ρ|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{-1}, where ψ ≠ 1 has p-power order (one of the (q−1)/2 non-Steinberg components in footnote 5). It has two minimal-conductor twists by characters ≡ 1 mod ϖ, namely ρ⊗ψ (ψ² ⊕ 1 on I_v) and ρ⊗ψ^{-1} (1 ⊕ ψ^{-2} on I_v). These two twists are not related by an unramified twist. The correct statement is: uniqueness holds except when v ≡ 1 mod p and either ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible (harmless) or ρ̄|G_v is, up to unramified twist, a ramified non-split extension of 1 by 1 (case (3)). The candidate's correction of the claim is right and minimal. Its assessment of the consequences is not. The proof also needs the twisting map (eigenforms in S_φ) → (points of R_φ) to be injective, and at case-(3) primes it is not. Primes of type (3) therefore need a separate treatment in the proof of Theorem 4.8. For example, one could use at v the ring of lifts with conductor exponent ≤ 1 and p-power inertial determinant, taken over O[Δ_v], instead of R_{v,φ}, or handle these primes differently from the ψ^{-1/2} twist.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this from scratch using the page images (PDF pp. 65–70).

**Setup.** R_{v,φ} is the full fixed-determinant ring. For non-harmless v, χ_φ|I_v is trivial (φ is ramified only at harmless primes). In case (3), after an unramified twist, ρ̄|G_v = (1 *; 0 1) with * ramified.

**The non-Steinberg lifts exist.** Take ρ(σ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}) with ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order dividing v−1, and ρ(Frob) = a·I. Then ρ(σ)^v = ρ(σ). The lift reduces to (1 1; 0 1), and its determinant is unramified and adjustable through a. For example p=3, v=7, ζ a cube root of 1. The paper itself describes these points on p. 365 ("χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order") and in footnote 5 (the (q−1)/2 components).

**Twists of such a lift.** Let η ≡ 1 mod ϖ, so ρ⊗η still lifts ρ̄. Then ρ⊗η has conductor exponent 1 = a(ρ̄) exactly when η|I_v ∈ {ψ, ψ^{-1}}. That gives two minimal twists. They differ by ψ², which is ramified and nontrivial because p is odd. So neither "uniquely twist equivalent" nor the claimed ring isomorphism holds. The ring statement fails under either reading:
- If "conductor-minimal" fixes the determinant up to unramified twist, it gives only the Steinberg component, one of (q+1)/2.
- If the determinant is free, it gives q components mapping 2:1 onto the non-Steinberg ones.

**Impact on the proof.** This is more than motivation. Take a newform f ∈ S_{φ,m} with ρ_f|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ η, η ≠ 1 (the paper needs such forms: every component of R_{v,φ} must be in the support of S_φ). Let Θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order with Θ|I_v = η^{-1}, and let g = f⊗Θ. Then:
- g has the same level N*, is still ordinary, and lies in the same m.
- χ_g|Φ = χ_f|Φ = φ, because Θ is trivial on the harmless part.
- ψ_g = ψ_f Θ², so ρ_g⊗ψ_g^{-1/2} = ρ_f⊗ψ_f^{-1/2}.
- ρ_g ≇ ρ_f, since the inertial types 1⊕η^{-1} and 1⊕η differ, so g and f have different T_l eigenvalues for some l.

So two points of Spec T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] map to one point of Spec R_φ[1/p]. Hence R_φ → T^an_{φ,m} is not surjective, and the asserted R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is false whenever such a prime occurs. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365): U_p eigenvalues also agree after the twist. The 2:1 fibres are exactly what the "uniqueness" claim was meant to rule out.

**Status of Theorem 4.8.** The theorem is probably still true via a double-cover local ring, which is still a complete intersection. So only the proof is affected. I did not build an explicit global ρ̄ satisfying the scalar hypothesis with a case-(3) prime. I disagree with the reader's "affects: nothing". 1. The claim is false.

Case (3) primes are non-harmless because ρ̄|G_v is reducible. Take v ≡ 1 mod p with ρ̄|G_v ≅ (unramified) ⊗ (1 *; 0 1), * ramified. p. 365 (Lemma 4.11) itself says the generic fibre of R_{v,φ} contains lifts 'χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{-1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order'. Footnote 5 says it has (q+1)/2 components.

- A twist ρ⊗θ with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ has conductor exponent 1 (minimal) exactly when θ|I_v = ψ or θ|I_v = ψ^{-1}.
- These two twists differ by ψ², which is ramified. Since p is odd and ψ ≠ 1, ψ² ≠ 1 and ψ² ≠ ψ^{-2}. So the minimal twist is not unique, not even up to unramified twist.
- The rings do not match either. The conductor-minimal ring with free determinant has 1 + (q−1) = q generic components (Steinberg, and θ ⊕ 1 for each θ ≠ 1). With determinant fixed to χ_φ|G_v, which is unramified here, it has only the Steinberg component. R_{v,φ} has (q+1)/2. So no reading of 'isomorphic up to unramified twists' works.
- Cross-check of the other v ≡ 1 mod p cases: in case (1), ρ̄|I_v ≅ χ̄ ⊕ 1, the other twist would be by a character ≡ χ̄^{-1} ≠ 1 mod ϖ, so uniqueness holds. The paper's exception list is therefore incomplete exactly by case (3).

2. Defence attempted.

Read 'conductor-minimal deformation ring' charitably, as 'lifts with determinant χ_φ that are twists of level-Γ_1(N) lifts'. Then sentence 1 is tautologically R_{v,φ}. But the 'Equivalently ... uniquely' sentence cannot be saved: uniqueness is exactly the property the authors use to separate harmless primes, where every twist has conductor 2.

3. Consequences: the passage is load-bearing.

- Uniqueness is what makes f ↦ ρ_f ⊗ ψ_f^{-1/2} injective from eigenforms in S_φ to points of R_φ. Given two such forms f, f', the twisted representations coincide iff ρ_{f'} = ρ_f⊗θ, with θ ≡ 1 mod ϖ ramified only at non-harmless primes. Uniqueness at each such prime forces θ to be unramified everywhere, so θ = 1.
- Case (3) breaks this. Let θ be a Dirichlet character of conductor v and p-power order, and let f1 ∈ S_φ be ordinary with ρ_{f1}|I_v ≅ θ ⊕ 1. Such f1 exists by the paper's own claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ. Set f2 = f1⊗θ^{-1}. Then ρ_{f2}|I_v ≅ 1 ⊕ θ^{-1}, which still has conductor exponent 1. The nebentypus of f2 is χ1θ^{-2}, and its restriction to Φ is still φ. So f2 ∈ S_φ, it is ordinary, and it lies in the m-part.
- Computation: ψ2 = ψ1θ^{-2}. Since the square root is unique in a p-group with p odd, ψ2^{-1/2} = ψ1^{-1/2}θ. Hence ρ_{f2}⊗ψ2^{-1/2} = ρ_{f1}⊗ψ1^{-1/2}. The twisted U_p-eigenvalues also agree.
- So f1 and f2 have distinct Hecke eigensystems: a_l(f2) = θ^{-1}(l)·a_l(f1), and the nebentypus at v is θ versus θ^{-1}. Yet they give the same Q̄_p-point of R_φ, and of R̃.
- Therefore R_φ[1/p] → T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] is not surjective, and the asserted isomorphism R_φ[1/p] ≃ T^an_{φ,m}[1/p] (p. 363) is false whenever N has a case-(3) prime. The same holds for R̃ ≃ T_{φ,m} (p. 365).
- The conclusions drawn from it are then unproven in that case: T_{φ,m} Cohen–Macaulay with dim ω/m = 3, hence the same for T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ], hence dim J_1(N*)[m] = 2.
- Lemma 4.11 treats case (3) explicitly, and Theorem 4.8 does not exclude it.

The statement of Theorem 4.8 is not shown false. The repair looks plausible: use a conductor-≤1 local ring over O[Δ_v] that should be Cohen–Macaulay. So I rate affects as 'the proof', not 'nothing' as the candidate proposed. Confidence is high that the passage is wrong, and medium-high on the exact extent of the damage to the proof.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 364, proof of Lemma 4.11: "Proof There are three cases in which R_v is not smooth. In two of these cases, we shall prove that R_v is a power series ring over O[Δ] for some finite cyclic abelian p-group Δ. [...] In the other case, we will show that R_v is a quotient of a power series ring by a single relation. [...] The three situations in which R_v is not smooth correspond to primes v such that: (1) v ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄|G_v is reducible, and ρ̄|I_v ≃ χ ⊕ 1 for some ramified χ. (2) v ≡ −1 mod p, ρ̄|G_v is absolutely irreducible and induced from a character ξ. (3) v ≡ 1 mod p, ρ̄^{I_v} is 1-dimensional and ρ̄^{ss}|G_v is unramified." p. 365: "Closed points on the generic fiber of R_{v,φ} correspond to lifts ρ of ρ̄|G_v which are either unramified twists of the Steinberg representation or lifts which decompose (after inverting p) into a sum χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{−1} with ψ|I_v of p-power order." Footnote 5: "The generic fibre of R_v has (q + 1)/2 geometric components, where q is the largest power of p dividing v − 1 (see also Theorem 1.0.1(A2.2) of [55])." arXiv v2 has the same text.
sourceIssues.correction: The list of non-smooth cases is incomplete. A fourth case is missing: v ≡ −1 mod p and ρ̄|G_v ≅ μ⊗(ω̄ *; 0 1) with μ unramified and * ramified (the mod-p Steinberg representation). Equivalently, case (3) should read "v ≡ ±1 mod p". The case-(3) argument still works, but one sentence has to change: when v ≡ −1, the non-Steinberg closed points of the generic fibre are not of the form χ_φψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}. They are Ind from Q_{v²} of a tame character ψ, where ψ|I_v has order q' > 1, a power of p dividing v+1. H²(G_v, ad⁰ρ) = 0 at every such point, so R_v ≅ O⟦x1,…,x4⟧/(r) with r ≠ 0, and R_v[1/p] is formally smooth. In footnote 5, q is then the largest power of p dividing v+1; in general, the p-part of v²−1. The relation r = C(T) − T still works. Lemma 4.11 as stated remains true.

I transcribed the text from 220-dpi renders of PDF pp. 68–69 (pp. 364–365). Setup: v ≠ p, p odd, and R_v is the unrestricted framed deformation ring with fixed determinant. By the local Euler characteristic, dim Z^1 = 3 + h^2(ad^0ρ̄). So R_v is not smooth exactly when H^0(G_v, ad^0ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Redoing the classification for ρ̄ minimal among twists gives four cases, not three:
- v≡1, split, χ ramified.
- v≡−1, induced from the unramified quadratic extension.
- v≡1, ramified unipotent.
- v≡−1, ρ̄ ≅ μ⊗(ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified.
The fourth case is missing. It is minimal: the conductor exponent is 1 and no twist lowers it. In this case e = (0 1; 0 0) spans H^0(ad^0ρ̄(1)), because G_v acts on it by ω̄^2 and ω̄(Frob_v) = −1. Also H^0(ad^0ρ̄) = 0: e is inertia-fixed, but Frobenius acts on it by −1. So h^2 = 1 and dim Z^1 = 4. That exceeds the relative dimension 3, so R_v is not formally smooth.

I checked the extra lifts. Take ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{−1}) with ζ ≠ 1, ζ^{v+1} = 1, of p-power order, and S = (d1, (d2−d1)/δ; d1δ, −d1) with δ = ζ^{−1}−ζ. Then S ρ(τ) S^{−1} = ρ(τ)^v; I verified this numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19). Taking d1 ≡ −1 and d2−d1 ∈ δO, the lift reduces to ρ̄. Hensel's lemma lets det S hit the fixed determinant.

Lemma 4.11 itself still holds. At Steinberg points H^0(ad^0ρ(1)) = 0, since Frobenius acts on e by v^{±2} ≠ 1. At the induced points, ad^0ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)⊗ε. Frobenius acts on ηε by −v^{±1}, and the second summand has no inertia invariants because ζ^2 ≠ 1.

I believe such ρ̄ exist within the §4.1 scope: unramified at p with scalar Frob_p (Thm 4.8). One route is an S4-quartic construction with p=3, v=2. I have not verified an explicit example. The submitter's elliptic-curve example is only local, since det ρ̄_{E,3} is ramified at 3.

The submitter says the case-(3) argument covers this "verbatim". That is not quite right: the description of the generic points has to change.

Lemma 4.11 is used only in the proof of Thm 4.8 (p. 363); grep finds no other citations. There is a related, more serious flaw that should be a separate item. On p. 363 the paper claims that for non-harmless v every lift is twist-equivalent to a conductor-minimal one, and that the only exception is v≡1 with ρ̄ having trivial I_v-invariants. The induced lifts above have conductor v^2 and cannot be twisted down to conductor v. So the claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*)) fails at such v. The likely repair is to use the smooth Steinberg quotient at such v. So I rate this as affecting the proof, not the stated results.

Minor side point: in footnote 5, "primitive q-th root of unity" should be "q-th root of unity ζ ≠ 1". Otherwise the count (q−1)/2 is wrong when q = p^2. Setting. By p. 365 of the paper, p ≥ 3 and v ≠ p. R_v is the unrestricted framed ring with fixed determinant. Here χ_φ|G_v is unramified at every v that is not harmless. The only condition the paper imposes at v | N is that ρ̄ has minimal conductor among its twists, and the mod-p Steinberg type (conductor exponent 1) satisfies it. The local Euler characteristic gives dim Z¹(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h²(ad⁰ρ̄) − h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) + h⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 3 + h⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)). R_v has relative dimension 3, so it fails to be formally smooth exactly when H⁰(G_v, ad⁰ρ̄(1)) ≠ 0.

Missing case. Take v ≡ −1 mod p and ρ̄ = (ω̄ *; 0 1) with * ramified. Such an extension exists and is unique: h¹(G_v, ω̄) = h⁰(ω̄) + h⁰(ω̄^{-1}·ω̄) = 0 + 1, and the unramified part is ω̄/(Frob−1) = 0. Conjugating by the unipotent ρ̄(τ) shows H⁰(I_v, ad⁰ρ̄) = k·e with e = (0 1; 0 0), since p is odd. Frobenius acts on e by ω̄(Frob) = −1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄) = 0. On e⊗ω̄ it acts by (−1)(−1) = 1, so H⁰(ad⁰ρ̄(1)) = k·e. Hence h² = 1, dim Z¹ = 4 > 3, and R_v is not smooth. This case is none of (1)–(3): v ≢ 1, and ρ̄|G_v is reducible.

Checks. I brute-forced H⁰ over F_p. It has dimension 1 for (p,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (5,19), (7,13). It has dimension 0 for v ≢ ±1, e.g. (5,7) and (7,5). Redoing the classification (irreducible, split, and non-split types) gives exactly four non-smooth twist-minimal cases, so only this one is missing.

Lemma 4.11 survives. The lifts are of two kinds.
- Steinberg twists. H⁰(ad⁰ρ(1)) = 0 because Frobenius acts on e by v² ≠ 1.
- The extra points, with ρ(τ) = (ζ 1; 0 ζ^{-1}), ζ^{v+1} = 1, ζ ≠ 1 of p-power order, and ρ(σ) = S swapping the eigenlines. I checked S·T = T^v·S numerically for (q,v) = (3,2), (3,5), (3,11), (9,17), (5,19), (3,8), (9,26). These lifts reduce to ρ̄. Here ad⁰ρ(1) = ηε ⊕ Ind(ψ/ψ^σ)ε. Frobenius acts on the first summand by −v ≠ 1. The second has no inertia invariants, since ζ^{±2} ≠ 1.

So the error is in the proof only. The submitted corrections are right. H-part1b-2 says the argument covers the new case "verbatim", which is slightly off: the generic-point description must change. X-K5-8's correction states it correctly.

Could the case be excluded? Nothing in §4.1 rules it out. Examples plausibly exist: take the mod-3 reduction of an odd octahedral Artin representation (projective image S4 ≅ PGL2(F3)) that is tamely ramified of index 3 at some v ≡ 2 mod 3, with 3 split completely. Projectively, D_v = S3 is the Borel subgroup, and this forces ρ̄|G_v to be of the missing type. I have not verified an explicit example.

Consequences. Lemma 4.11 is cited only in the proof of Thm 4.8, on p. 363, and it is used implicitly on p. 365 through Lemma 4.2. The consequence is serious but separate, and it deserves its own item, distinct from C-K5-0. For this local type, p ∤ v−1, so no nebentypus twist is available at v. The Ind components have conductor v² and cannot be twisted down. So the p. 363 claim that every component of R_{v,φ} lies in the support of S_φ (level Γ1(N*), v ∥ N*) fails at such v. The natural repair is to use the minimally ramified (Steinberg) quotient there, which is formally smooth (CHT §2.4). The stated results are unaffected.

sourceIssues.reason:
I redid the computation. Set t^v + t^{−v} − t − t^{−1} = (t^v − t)(1 − t^{−v−1}). So C(T) = T at T = t + t^{−1} exactly when t^{v−1} = 1 or t^{v+1} = 1. C(T) − T is separable of degree v in T: its roots are ±2, (v−3)/2 values from t^{v−1} = 1 and (v−1)/2 values from t^{v+1} = 1. The condition T − 2 ∈ m forces t ≡ 1, so t is a 1-unit root of unity of p-power order. Since v ≡ 1 mod p and p is odd, p does not divide v + 1, so t^{v+1} = 1 gives only t = 1, and t^{v−1} = 1 gives t ∈ μ_q.

The T-values in the residue disc are therefore T = 2 plus ζ + ζ^{−1} for ζ ∈ μ_q \ {1} modulo inversion. That is 1 + (q−1)/2 = (q+1)/2 values, matching the footnote's count. Each ζ ≠ 1 gives one geometric component: σ is regular semisimple with eigenvalues ζ^{±1}, Frobenius lies in its centralizer torus with fixed determinant, and the result is irreducible of dimension 3.

If only primitive ζ were allowed there would be φ(q)/2 = p^{s−1}(p−1)/2 such components, fewer than (q−1)/2 once q = p^s with s ≥ 2. Concrete check: p = 3, v = 19, so q = 9. ζ_3 + ζ_3^{−1} = −1 satisfies T − 2 = −3 ∈ m and is a genuine root, giving 4 = (9−1)/2 non-trivial values against 3 primitive ones.

The sentence itself points the same way. It says "finitely ramified of order dividing q", and "ζ ≠ 1" would be redundant for a primitive q-th root, since q ≥ p > 1. So "primitive" is a slip. The counts (q+1)/2 and (q−1)/2 are correct; only this adjective is wrong. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. (That known defect does appear on the same page in "R_v ≅ O[x1,…,x4]/(r)", which should read O⟦x1,…,x4⟧/(r), but that is separate.)

sourceIssues.locator: §4.1, proof of Theorem 4.8, p. 366 (published version)
sourceIssues.printed: (p. 366, PDF p. 70, checked on the page image) "If T_m is the Hecke ring at full level Γ_1(N*), then the restriction map induces an inclusion map T_m ↪ ⊕ T_{φ^2,m} ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕ O(φ). Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Because the map above is an isomorphism after tensoring with K, and since all the relevant spaces of modular forms are ϖ-torsion free, we have an isomorphism T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O[Φ]. Hence, applying Lemma 4.2 once more, we deduce that T_m is Cohen–Macaulay and dim ω_{T_m}/m = 3"
sourceIssues.correction:
The isomorphism T_m ≃ T_{1,m} ⊗_O O[Φ] is true, but the proof should use generators.

Embed T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] in ⊕_φ T_{1,m} by t⊗[g] ↦ (φ(g)t)_φ. Identify S_{φ²,m} with S_{1,m} by twisting by φ, where φ is viewed as a Dirichlet character mod M through the projection (Z/N*Z)^× → Φ, g ↦ ḡ. Then:
- T_l, and U_l, U_p for l ∤ M, map to (φ(l)T_l)_φ = T_l ⊗ [l̄].
- U_l for l | M is 0 on the m-part, since every lift is supercuspidal at harmless l.
- ⟨d⟩ maps to ⟨d⟩ ⊗ [d̄]².

So the image lies in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. This replaces "since T_m is local".

For d in Φ ⊂ (Z/N*Z)^×, ⟨d⟩ acts trivially on S_1, so ⟨d⟩ maps to 1 ⊗ [d]². Since |Φ| is odd, squaring is a bijection of Φ, so every 1 ⊗ [g] is in the image. Then T_l ⊗ 1 = (T_l ⊗ [l̄])(1 ⊗ [l̄]⁻¹) is in the image. Together with the surjection T_m → T_{1,m}, this shows the map is onto. This replaces "isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free", which gives only injectivity.

Two smaller points:
1. The argument needs ⟨d⟩ ∈ T_m. This is not automatic, because T is generated by the T_l for primes l. It holds for p odd because det = (tr² − tr(g²))/2 for the pseudo-character.
2. T_m, a Z_p-algebra, should be read as T_m ⊗_{W(k_m)} O.

The fix proposed in X-K5-11 is right with the + signs (its ± is harmless), and it is minimal. H-part1b-5 gives the same argument.
sourceIssues.reason:
This is confirmed on the page image, and arXiv v2 has the same wording. O[Φ] is the group ring of a finite group, so it is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Both justifications given in the paper fail:
(1) Being local does not force the image into T_{1,m}⊗O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m}=O, Φ=Z/p and O=Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A={(a_φ)∈⊕O : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ[g], which is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p)=p−1≥2.
(2) An injection of ϖ-torsion-free lattices that becomes an isomorphism after ⊗K need not be onto. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself an example. Torsion-freeness gives only injectivity.
So the printed reasons prove at most an inclusion of finite index. I checked the candidate's replacement argument myself, including the twisting convention, the images T_l ↦ T_l⊗[l] and ⟨d⟩ ↦ 1⊗[d]^2 for d∈Φ, and that squaring is bijective on Φ. It is correct, apart from the small base-change caveat noted in the correction.
On 'affects', I disagree with the candidate's "nothing". The proof of Theorem 4.8 as printed does not establish the isomorphism, and a different argument is needed, so it affects the proof. Theorem 4.8 still holds, because the intermediate isomorphism is true. Only the multiplicity-two statement of Thm 4.8 uses this step, together with Remark 4.12 ("a similar argument"), and neither is changed. I tried to defend the printed argument and could not.

(1) "Since T_m is local, the image lands inside T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]" does not follow. A local subring of T_{1,m} ⊗ ⊕_φ O need not lie in T_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ]. Take T_{1,m} = O, Φ = Z/p, O = Z_p[ζ_p]. The ring A = {(a_φ) : all a_φ congruent mod ϖ} is local and contains O[Φ]. It also contains (ϖ,0,…,0) = (ϖ/p)Σ_g[g], and this is not in O[Φ] because v_ϖ(p) = p−1 ≥ 2. The containment is true only because of the explicit images of the generators, and the paper never states them.

(2) "Isomorphism after ⊗K + ϖ-torsion free" gives only an injection of lattices of the same rank. O[Φ] ⊂ ⊕_φ O is itself such an injection, and it is not onto.

I looked for other readings:
- a Nakayama argument would need surjectivity onto target/m_{T_m}·target, not just onto the residue field;
- an integral module isomorphism S_2(Γ_1(N*),O)_m ≅ S_{1,m} ⊗ O[Φ] would still leave the same generator argument to be made;
- nothing elsewhere in the paper supplies the step (I searched every twisting passage and the 2022 Correction).

sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered PDF pp. 71–72 (pp. 367–368) and the text is exactly as quoted. arXiv v2 (p. 52–53) has the same wording. Each point in the candidate holds.
(a) A Noetherian semi-local ring is not in general the product of its localizations. For example, Z_(p) is not Q × Z_(p). What makes it work is dimension 0. The paper has that one sentence earlier: Spec R[1/p] is in bijection with Spec of a finite product of fields, so every prime is maximal. So "semi-local" names the wrong property, and "finite ideals" is a misprint for "(finitely many) prime ideals". "Direct sum" is harmless because there are finitely many factors.
(b) "G_{L,S} has finite image in G_{F,S}" is literally false: the image is an open subgroup of finite index and is infinite in general. It should say "finite index".
(c) The step needs the restriction H^1(G_{F,S}, ad V) → H^1(G_{L,S}, ad V) to be injective. By inflation–restriction its kernel is H^1(Gal(L/F), (ad V)^{G_L}), which is 0 because the group is finite and the coefficients are in characteristic zero. That is exactly what the paper's parenthetical describes. Inflation is always injective on H^1 and is not the relevant map. Even on a generous reading with an arbitrary L, where G_{L,S} → G_{F,S} factors as a surjection onto a finite-index subgroup, the kernel of H^1 of a finite group comes from restriction.
(d) "unramified outside primes outside those above S" has a doubled "outside". Read literally it contradicts the next clause, "unramified at all primes v|p", because S has no primes above p. Also, the image is Z_p^r, not necessarily Z_p. The step itself is fine: in a torsion-free abelian pro-p extension, inertia at v∤p has finite image and is therefore trivial. So an extension unramified at p is unramified everywhere, hence finite, hence trivial.
I re-checked the rest of the proof and it is correct: R[1/p] → A/m² is surjective since 𝔭 is maximal, and the traces argument goes through. Lemma 4.14 is cited only in the introduction (p. 298, comparison with Buzzard–Taylor) and in the remark right after it. No later theorem uses it. So these are wording slips in a correct proof of a correct lemma, and none of them is one of the 47 known bracket errors.

Under the intended reading (8) is redundant, and the omission changes nothing. Caveat: if 'irreducible' is read as absolutely irreducible, ρ̄|I_v is never irreducible at v|p (inertia acts through an abelian tame quotient or reducibly), and (8) is harmless as printed. So a lift is compared with the Teichmüller lifts, not with ψ itself. Conjecture A(2)(b) on p. 374 likewise reads "If ρ̄|D_v is of type P, so that ρ̄|I_v ≅ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}". The only coherent reading of (c) therefore has ρ̄.

Under that reading the hypothesis is the natural one. det ρ̄ is the mod-p cyclotomic character, which is unramified at x ∤ p. So when ρ̄|D_x is reducible and ρ̄|I_x is semisimple, the two inertial characters are automatically inverse to each other. Adding the bar changes no statement or argument. Everything later (conditions (5) to (8), Conjecture A, and the §5 theorems) already uses ρ̄ for this case.
