sourceIssues.printed: p. 404: "primes which exactly annihilate the dual Selmer group, which is H^1_{L*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(F, μ_p). This group sits inside H^1(F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}, by Hilbert's Theorem 90 in the classical version."
sourceIssues.correction: H^1_{L*}(F, μ_p) = H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p).
sourceIssues.reason: Over the field F of characteristic 0, μ_p is étale. So H^1_fppf(F, μ_p) = H^1(F, μ_p) = F^×/F^{×p}, which is infinite and is the whole group, not something that "sits inside" it. The dual Selmer group is cut out by the conditions L*_v. At finite v∤p these are the unramified (unit) classes, and at v|p they are the annihilator of the unramified classes, i.e. O_v^×/O_v^{×p}, the finite flat classes. This is {x ∈ F^×/F^{×p} : v(x) ≡ 0 mod p for all v}, which equals H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p). The paper itself says this on p. 402: "So we are interested in H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p), which sits in the exact sequence 0 → O_F^×/O_F^{×p} → H^1_fppf(O_F, μ_p) → Cl(F)[p] → 0". So O_F was meant, and the slip is clear from context.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 405: "Our patching result then allows us to deduce that there is an isomorphism R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F) ⊗ Z_p], and hence an isomorphism between the Galois group of the maximal unramified abelian p-power extension of F and the class group of F."

sourceIssues.reason: The Galois group of the maximal unramified abelian p-power extension is a finite p-group. Here ζ_p ∉ F forces p odd, so the real places do not matter. By class field theory this group is Cl(F) ⊗ Z_p = Cl(F)[p^∞], not the whole class group. Taken literally, the sentence is false whenever Cl(F) has torsion prime to p. The displayed isomorphism R^unr ≃ Z_p[Cl(O_F) ⊗ Z_p] just before it shows that the p-part is meant. This is informal expository text, so no stated result depends on it. The single bracket in Z_p[...] is a separate matter: for a finite group the group ring Z_p[G] is correct anyway, and it is not part of this candidate.

sourceIssues.locator: §8.4 "The invariant l_0", published p. 406 (PDF p. 110): the paragraph defining "odd" and the two displays that follow, ending with equation (1). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §8.4, pp. 80–81) has word-for-word the same text. arXiv v1 has no GL(n)/§8 material. Prop. 8.5(4) (p. 410) uses the result through "The last property then follows from Proposition 8.4, equation (1)…" (p. 411).
sourceIssues.printed: Let V be a representation of G_F of dimension n over a field of characteristic different from 2, and assume that the action of G_{F_v} is *odd* for each v|∞. Explicitly, this is the trivial condition for complex places, and for real places v|∞ says that the action of complex conjugation c_v ∈ G_{F_v} satisfies Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}. Then, via an elementary calculation, one has: Σ_{v|∞} dim H^0(F_v, ad^0(V)) = { r_1((n^2+1)/2 − 1) + r_2(n^2 − 1), n odd; r_1(n^2/2 − 1) + r_2(n^2 − 1), n even. } Thus, in both cases we see that: Σ_{v|∞} dim H^0(F_v, ad^0(V)) = [F : Q] n(n−1)/2 + l_0.   (1)
sourceIssues.correction: Change "satisfies Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1, 0, 1}" to "has ±1-eigenspaces whose dimensions differ by at most 1". This is equivalent to Trace(c_v) ∈ {−1,0,1} only in characteristic 0 or in characteristic ℓ > n+1 (n even), resp. ℓ > n (n odd). Alternatively, keep the trace criterion and restrict V to those characteristics. Under the §8.5 standing assumption p > n, the only bad case is n even with p = n+1. Optionally, the proof of Prop. 8.5(4) can cite the inequality Σ_{v|∞} h^0(F_v, ad^0 V) ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0, which holds for every V with no parity hypothesis, in place of equation (1).
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered PDF p. 110 and transcribed the text as above. Setup: c_v^2 = 1 and char ≠ 2, so c_v is diagonalisable with eigenspace dimensions a, b (a + b = n). Its centraliser in ad has dimension a^2 + b^2 and contains elements of trace 1. Hence dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a^2 + b^2 − 1 = (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1, where d = a − b. The printed formula is the case |d| ≤ 1. In characteristic ℓ, however, Trace(c_v) = d mod ℓ.

Counterexample (within the printed hypotheses): F = Q, n = 2, coefficient field F_3, V with c acting trivially. Then Trace(c) = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V counts as "odd". But dim H^0(R, ad^0 V) = dim ad^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n^2/2 − 1) = 1. Also l_0 = r_1(n−2)/2 = 0, so the right side of (1) is 1·1 + 0 = 1 ≠ 3.

A Python sweep over n ≤ 14 and primes ℓ < 40 confirms that the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n + 1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). With p > n, the failures are (n, p) = (2,3), (4,5), (6,7), (10,11), (12,13), … The case matters for the paper: §8.5 imposes "r̄|_{G_v} is odd" on r̄ : G_F → GL_n(k) with p > n. For example, n = 4, p = 5, r̄(c_v) = ±I has trace ±4 ≡ ∓1 mod 5. It is also compatible with the determinant, since ε^{6}(c_v) = 1. So r̄ meets the printed hypothesis, but (1) fails for it (15 versus 7 per real place).

How far it reaches: Theorem 5.16(5) defines oddness for O-valued (characteristic-0) representations, where the trace criterion is correct. Its residual r̄ then has the same eigenspace dimensions, so the main theorems are unaffected. The proof of Prop. 8.5(4) invokes (1), but it only needs Σ h^0 ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0. That inequality holds for every involution, since (n^2 + d^2)/2 − 1 is smallest at |d| ≤ 1. A larger h^0 only lowers the variable count, and a quotient of a power series ring in fewer variables is a quotient of one in more. So Prop. 8.5(4) remains true. The false statement is confined to the displayed formula and equation (1) (and the "Explicitly…" gloss) in small characteristic. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Suppose c_v has ±1-eigenspaces of dimensions a and b, with a + b = n. Then dim H^0(F_v, ad^0 V) = a² + b² − 1 in any characteristic other than 2, and Trace(c_v) = a − b computed in the field. In characteristic ℓ the trace condition only forces a − b ≡ −1, 0, 1 (mod ℓ).

Counterexample: take F = Q, n = 2, ℓ = 3 and V trivial, so c = I. Then Trace = 2 = −1 in F_3, so V is "odd" as printed. But Σ dim H^0 = 3, while the display gives r_1(n²/2 − 1) = 1, and (1) gives [F:Q]·1 + l_0 = 1 + 0 = 1.

This also happens inside §8.5's setting: n = 4, p = 5, F = Q, r̄(c) = ±I. The trace is ±4 = ∓1 in F_5, and det = 1 = ε(c)^6 matches ξ = ε^6. Here Σ h^0 = 15, but (1) gives 7.

A brute-force check over n ≤ 12 and primes ℓ < 40 shows the trace criterion fails exactly when ℓ ≤ n+1 (n even) or ℓ ≤ n (n odd). So the candidate's description is right.

Defence attempted:
- The only earlier definition of "odd" (p. 383) is for O-valued representations. There the trace is the integer a − b, and the criterion is correct.
- For a field of characteristic ℓ, the "Explicitly…" sentence is the only definition given. The text explicitly allows any characteristic other than 2, so the literal claim is false. Reading "Trace" as the integer a − b is not supported by the text.

Consequences (checked on the page images):
- Equation (1) is used only in the proof of Prop. 8.5(4). The variable count there is h^1_{L,T} + Σ_T h^0(ad) − h^0(ad) = q + |T| − 1 − Σ_{v|∞} h^0(ad^0 r̄), using Prop. 8.4.
- For every V, a² + b² ≥ its value when |a − b| ≤ 1. So Σ_{v|∞} h^0(F_v, ad^0 V) ≥ [F:Q]n(n−1)/2 + l_0 always, and the true count is at most the stated g.
- A quotient of R_loc⟦x_1..x_m⟧ with m ≤ g is also a quotient of R_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧. So Prop. 8.5(4) is true as stated, with or without oddness.
- Thm 9.19 uses Prop. 8.5 only to choose surjections R^i_∞ = R_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧ ↠ R^□_{S_{Q_N}}. Their dimensions come from Lemma 8.2, so it is unaffected.
- Thm 5.16(5) assumes the O-valued r is odd, which forces r̄ to have balanced eigenspaces (p odd), so equation (1) holds there.

So the reach is limited to the display and equation (1) themselves. No numbered statement is affected. The mathematics is right with the intended notion of "odd", and the correction above is the minimal fix.

sourceIssues.correction: (1) should read: "Each of R^1_loc and R^χ_loc is equidimensional of dimension 1 + |S_p ∪ R|(n^2 − 1) + [F:Q]n(n−1)/2, and all of its minimal primes have characteristic 0." This is what [11, Prop. 3.1] and [76, Lemma 3.3](2),(3),(5) actually give. On p. 426, likewise replace "p-torsion free" with "has all minimal primes of characteristic 0". sourceIssues.reason:
Printed text confirmed from the page images. The cited sources do not give flatness. [11] is Taylor, IHES 108. I checked Prop. 3.1 in the author copy (…/agents/k8check/twugkfin.txt). It says only: Spec R^loc/I^χ is irreducible, its generic point has characteristic 0, and it has dimension n^2+1; for R^loc/I^{(1,…,1)}, all components have dimension n^2+1 and characteristic-0 generic points. Its proof shows only (R^loc/I^χ)_red is O-flat. Only the separate Steinberg quotient is "by definition flat over O". [76, Lemma 3.3] is BLGHT, CY II (…/k8check/cy2fin.txt). Its part 3 assumes O-flat inputs, and parts 5 and 7 are about minimal primes.

The statement is also false. Take n ≥ 2, p > n, v ∈ R with r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p; this is the intended Ihara-avoidance setting. Let Φ = ρ(φ_v) and Σ = ρ(σ_v) be the universal matrices over R^1_v, with φσφ^{-1} = σ^q in the tame quotient. Put N = log Σ; this is fine since (Σ−1)^n = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and n < p. Then ΦNΦ^{-1} = qN. Taking traces, tr(ΦN) = q·tr(ΦN), so (q−1)·tr(ΦN) = 0. For n = 2 simply N = Σ−1, S² = 0 and Σ^q = 1+qS.

Now tr(ΦN) ≠ 0. Take B = O⟦u⟧[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y) with c = ξ(φ_v) ≡ 1. Set Φ = diag(1+u, c/(1+u), 1, …) and Σ = diag(1+Y, 1−Y, 1, …), with σ_v^a ↦ diag(1+aY, 1−aY, …). This is a valid framed lift of determinant ξ. It reduces to 1, commutes, and Σ^q = Σ because (q−1)Y = 0. Every inertia element has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 − a²Y² = (X−1)^2 (times (X−1)^{n−2}). So there is a map R^1_v → B, and tr(ΦN) maps to ((1+u) − c/(1+u))·Y ≠ 0. This is because B ⊃ (O/(q−1))⟦u⟧·Y and the u-coefficient 1+c ≡ 2 is a unit.

So R^1_v has non-zero p-power torsion. The same holds for R^1_loc, via R^1_v → R^1_loc → B ⊗_O O' using O'-points of the other factors. Hence Lemma 8.2(1) fails for R^1_loc. For comparison, at points where Φ is regular semisimple the local ring is smooth ⊗ O[Y]/(Y², (q−1)Y), the same phenomenon.

The candidate is therefore genuine, and stronger than a gap: the claim is false. Downstream, only characteristic-0 minimal primes are used, so Theorem 9.19 stands after the repair. The cited sources give only characteristic-0 generic points, never p-torsion-freeness. I checked this in the texts. Taylor [11, Prop. 3.1] states: for distinct χ, Spec R^loc_v/I^χ is irreducible with generic point of characteristic zero; for (1,…,1), all components have dimension n^2+1 with characteristic-zero generic points. Its proof shows only that "(R^loc_v/I^χ)_red is flat over O". The only ring that is O-flat "by definition" is the separately saturated Steinberg quotient. BLGHT [76, Lemma 3.3](3) proves A⊗̂B is O-flat only for O-flat inputs. BLGHT's own use of the lemma for Taylor's ring R^{2T}_{χ,∞} derives irreducibility, dimensions and characteristic-0 generic points, never flatness. Taylor's main argument (p. 36) also asserts only these.

The claim is in fact false for R^1_loc. Take r̄|G_v trivial and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. This is exactly the setting of [11, §3], so the citation applies, and N(v) ≡ 1 mod p is already required for v ∈ R. Take n = 2 and write Φ = ρ(φ_v), Σ = 1 + S = ρ(σ_v). The condition char Σ = (X−1)^2 gives tr S = det S = 0, so S^2 = 0 by Cayley–Hamilton and Σ^q = 1 + qS. The tame relation ΦΣΦ^{-1} = Σ^q then gives ΦS = qSΦ. Taking traces, (1−q)·tr(ΦS) = 0 in R_v^1, where 1−q = p^s·unit with s ≥ 1.

Now tr(ΦS) ≠ 0 in R_v^1. The lift Φ = diag(1+X, δ/(1+X)) (δ = ξ(φ_v)) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α), valued in A = O⟦X⟧[α]/(α^2, (q−1)α), is a valid point of R_v^1:
- Σ^q = Σ, since (q−1)α = 0;
- every inertia element acts by diag(1+mα, 1−mα), which has characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 and determinant 1;
- det Φ = δ.
Under this point, tr(ΦS) maps to α((1+X) − δ/(1+X)). That is non-zero in (O/(q−1))⟦X⟧·α, and even modulo ϖ.

For general n with p > n, the same argument works with N = log Σ (so ΦN = qNΦ) and Σ = diag(1+α, 1−α, 1, …, 1). Since the other factors have O'-points, the p-torsion survives in R^1_loc = (⊗̂R_w)⊗̂(⊗̂R_v^1) and in R^1_∞. So (1) fails for R^1_loc whenever R ≠ ∅ in the cited setting, and even more so in the non-trivial cases raised in X-K8-12.

Defence attempt: read R_v^1 as the O-flat closure. That fails too. The torsion element is non-zero mod ϖ, so the flat closure's special fibre is a proper quotient of R_v^1/ϖ = R_v^χ/ϖ, and Noetherian rings are Hopfian, so (2) would then fail. §8.5.2 also makes the rings represent CHT-style deformation problems, which is the naive, non-saturated reading. For comparison, for n = 2 and trivial r̄ I checked that R_v^χ is O-flat: it is O⟦α,β,γ,u,y,z⟧ modulo the 2×2 minors and α^2+βγ−e, a hypersurface in an O-flat determinantal CM ring. So the defect is specific to R^1.

Consequences: Prop. 6.6 and Thm 6.3 need only dim R_∞ = 1+q+j−l_0, not torsion-freeness. The R^1 step (p. 428) explicitly uses only "all such primes have characteristic 0" plus [11, Lemma 2.2(2)]. The only place torsion-freeness enters is Theorem 6.4 for R^2_∞. There [11, Lemma 2.3] with Theorem 6.3(iii) and Lemma 8.2(3) gives near-faithfulness directly; the last paragraph of Theorem 6.4's proof is exactly this. So Theorem 9.19 survives with a local rerouting. Lemma 8.2(1) itself, a stated result, is false for R^1_loc. p-torsion-freeness of R^χ_loc for n ≥ 3 is unverified but not needed.

sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered PDF p. 111 and the printed text matches the candidate. Nothing in the Notation section restricts 'character' to finite order.

Counterexample: take n = 2 and p ≥ 3, and let v ∈ R. R may contain any prime with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p, so it can be nonempty. Since v ∤ p, the maximal pro-p quotient of I_v is Z_p(1), and Frobenius acts on it by t ↦ t^{q_v}. Let t be a generator. Define the continuous character χ_1 : I_v → Z_p(1) → 1 + pZ_p by t ↦ 1 + p, and set χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}. These are distinct characters with trivial product, so they are admissible as printed.

Now take a Q̄_p-point ρ of R_v^{χ_v}, choose σ ∈ I_v mapping to t, and let φ be a Frobenius lift. Then φσφ^{-1} ∈ I_v, and ρ(φσφ^{-1}) is conjugate to ρ(σ), so the two have the same characteristic polynomial. The defining condition then forces {x, x^{-1}} = {x^{c}, x^{-c}}, where x = 1 + p and c = q_v^{±1}, depending on which way Frobenius is normalized. But x has infinite order in Z_p^×, so this needs c = ±1, which is impossible because q_v ≥ 2. As a sanity check with p = 3 and q_v = 7: 4^7 = 16384 is neither 4 nor 4^{-1}. So R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0.

On the other hand, R_v^{χ_v} is not zero. Since r̄ is at worst unipotently ramified at v and det r̄ = ξ̄, r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its characteristic polynomial (X−1)^2 equals ∏(X − χ̄_i). Hence p^N R_v^{χ_v} = 0 for some N, with R_v^{χ_v} ≠ 0. The completed tensor product R^χ_loc is then killed by p^N and still surjects onto k. So it is nonzero and not p-torsion free, and Lemma 8.2(1) is false for this admissible choice.

The alternative reading, where R_v^{χ_v} is the maximal O-flat quotient, fails too. Then R_v^{χ_v} = 0, so R^χ_loc = 0, which breaks the dimension claim in (1) and also (2), because R^1_loc/ϖ ≠ 0.

Finite order is not enough on its own either. If p^2 ∤ q_v − 1, an order-p^2 character of I_v fails in the same way. The Frobenius-invariance supplied by ψ ∘ Art^{-1} is exactly what is missing.

The proof's citation, [11, Prop. 3.1] (Taylor), concerns characters of the residue field (via Art) and does not cover the printed generality. The main theorems are unaffected, since §9 only uses characters of k_v^× via Art (p. 413: 'ψ_v = χ_v'). But Lemma 8.2 as stated is false under the printed hypothesis. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The literal statement is false.

1. **Only certain characters of I_v can occur for a characteristic-zero lift.**
   - A continuous χ : I_v → 1 + m_O factors through the pro-p quotient Z_p(1) of tame inertia (v ∤ p). Write u_i = χ_{v,i}(t) for a generator t.
   - For a lift ρ over a finite extension of Q_p, ρ(φtφ^{-1}) = ρ(t^{q_v}) is conjugate to ρ(t). So the multiset {u_i^{q_v}} must equal {u_i}.
   - Hence some power u_i^{q_v^m − 1} = 1, so each u_i is a root of unity. For n = 2 and χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}, the condition forces u^{q_v − 1} = 1, i.e. χ factors through the p-part of k_v^×.
   - Counterexample: I_v ↠ Z_p(1) ≅ Z_p → 1 + pZ_p, t ↦ (1+p)^t, of infinite order. It is continuous, into 1 + m_O, distinct from its inverse, and the product is trivial, so it meets every printed condition.
   - Finite order is not enough either. With p = 3 and q_v = 7, the order-9 characters satisfy all printed conditions but are not Frobenius-stable. A script (work/agents/lensB-K8-11/chk.py) confirms the stable ones are exactly those with a(q_v − 1) ≡ 0 mod N.

2. **Lemma 8.2 then fails.** For such χ_v, R_v^{χ_v} has no Q̄_p-points, so R_v^{χ_v}[1/p] = 0 and the ring is killed by some p^N. It is still non-zero, because r̄|_{G_v} is a k-point: its inertia has characteristic polynomial (X − 1)^n, and ∏(X − χ_{v,i}(σ)) ≡ (X − 1)^n mod m_O. So R^χ_loc is non-zero and p-power torsion, and Lemma 8.2(1) ("p-torsion free and equidimensional of dimension …") fails. If R^χ_v is instead defined as the p-torsion-free closure of its Q̄_p-points, it is 0, and parts (1) and (2) fail anyway.

**Defence considered.** The notation section (p. 297) defines I_v ⊂ G_v as the full inertia group. So "characters of I_v" cannot faithfully be read as characters of the inertia of G_v^{ab}. The intended meaning can be recovered, but only from elsewhere:
- the proof of Lemma 8.2 cites [76, Lemma 3.3] and [11, Prop. 3.1], which are stated for characters of O_K^× via Art;
- §9.1 fixes ψ_v on (k_v^×)^n/(k_v^×);
- Conjecture B(3) uses ψ_{v,i}(Art_v^{-1}(σ)), and p. 415 identifies "ψ_v = χ_v".

So the defence fails for the statement as printed, but it shows the intended mathematics is correct.

**What depends on it.**
- Lemma 8.2 is used in Proposition 8.4/8.5 (R^χ_{S_Q}-type rings over R^χ_loc) and in the proof of Theorem 9.19 (pp. 425–427). There R^2_∞ = R^χ_loc⟦x_1..x_g⟧ is asserted p-torsion free, equidimensional and irreducible "by Lemma 8.2", and R^1_∞/ϖ ≅ R^2_∞/ϖ.
- Theorem 9.19 also uses "the local system associated to our choice of characters χ = (χ_v)", which only makes sense for characters of Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So the χ_v actually used are of the corrected form.

**Classification.** Main results unaffected; Lemma 8.2 needs a corrected hypothesis. I record this as an error in the hypothesis of a stated result. A reviewer could reasonably downgrade it to misprint/nothing, since §9 fixes the intended meaning.

**Side remark, not part of this candidate.** [11, Prop. 3.1] and Allen et al. §6.2.15 assume r̄|_{G_v} is trivial, while §8.5 only assumes unipotent ramification with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p.

sourceIssues.correction: Lemma 8.2 needs the hypothesis of [11, Prop 3.1]: for each v ∈ R, r̄|G_{F_v} is trivial. Allowing it up to an unramified scalar twist is harmless. Even then, [11] and [76, Lemma 3.3] give 'equidimensional of the stated dimension, and every minimal prime (generic point) has characteristic 0', not 'p-torsion free'. So (1) should be weakened to that unless flatness is proved separately. This weaker form is all that the proofs of Theorem 6.4 and Theorem 9.19 actually use. Because §8.5 requires R to contain every prime where r̄ ramifies, the triviality hypothesis cannot simply be added. Theorem 9.19/5.16 must instead do one of two things: (a) split R into primes where r̄|G_v is trivial, which get Taylor's R^1/R^χ, and the remaining primes, which get minimal or fixed-type local conditions whose rings are shown to be suitable (for example formally smooth when r̄|I_v is regular unipotent); or (b) first make r̄|G_v trivial at the primes of R by a solvable base change. The reader's proposed correction (add 'r̄|G_{F_v} trivial for all v ∈ R') is right, but by itself it is inconsistent with §8.5 and still leaves 'p-torsion free' unsupported.

I rendered PDF pp. 110–112 and read the printed text. Section 8.5 lets R be any finite set of primes that contains the ramified primes of r̄ and satisfies N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. Nothing requires r̄|G_v to be trivial for v ∈ R. Theorem 5.16(6) and Theorem 9.19 add no such condition either.

Counterexample to (3), checked from scratch. Take n = 2 (so p ≥ 3) and v ∈ R with r̄ unramified at v, r̄(Frob_v) with eigenvalues α ≠ β, and q = N(v) ≡ 1 mod p. Let O contain ζ_p. Take χ_1 a non-trivial p-power-order character of k_v^× (via Art) and χ_2 = χ_1^{-1}; these are distinct because p is odd.
- Every lift is split. Diagonalise r(Frob) = diag(A, B) by Hensel's lemma and write r(t) = 1 + M. By Cayley–Hamilton, the off-diagonal entries of (1+M)^q are c·M_12 and c·M_21, where c ≡ q ≡ 1 mod m. The relation Frob·t·Frob^{-1} = t^q gives (A/B − c)M_12 = 0, and A/B − c ≡ α/β − 1 is a unit, so M_12 = 0; likewise M_21 = 0. Wild inertia maps to a pro-p group, so it acts trivially.
- So r = γ_1 ⊕ γ_2 with γ_2 = ξγ_1^{-1}, and γ_1|I_v = γ_2|I_v^{-1} because ξ|I_v = 1. The element u = γ_1(t) = tr(r(t)P), where P = (r(Frob) − B)/(A − B), is well defined in R^{χ_v}_v.
- The characteristic-polynomial condition gives (u − χ_1(t))(u − χ_2(t)) = 0. Since χ_1(t) − χ_2(t) is a non-zero element of O, e = (u − χ_2(t))/(χ_1(t) − χ_2(t)) is an idempotent of R^χ_loc[1/p].
- e is neither 0 nor 1. Both loci have Q̄_p-points: γ_1 = (unramified lift of the α-character) × (extension of χ_i to G_v^ab), with γ_2 = ξγ_1^{-1}. For i = 1, 2 this has determinant ξ and inertial eigenvalues {χ_1(σ), χ_2(σ)}.
- Hence Spec R^χ_loc[1/p] is disconnected. If (1) and (3) both held, then p-torsion-freeness would put every minimal prime in characteristic 0, so Spec R^χ_loc[1/p] would be irreducible and hence connected. That is a contradiction. If another factor had no characteristic-0 points, (1) would fail instead.

Counterexample to (1) with the paper's literal definition, same v. The framed ring is R^□_v = O⟦X,a,b⟧[Y]/((1+Y)^{p^a} − 1), where p^a is the p-part of q − 1. The condition "char poly (X−1)^2 on I_v" is (1+Y) + (1+Y)^{-1} = 2, i.e. Y^2 = 0. So R^1_v = O⟦X,a,b⟧[Y]/(Y^2, p^aY), and p^{a−1}Y is a non-zero element killed by p.

A setup of this kind is realisable: Chebotarev gives primes ≡ 1 mod p with r̄(Frob) of distinct eigenvalues, and §8.5 lets such primes be added to R. The cited inputs ([11, Prop. 3.1]; BLGHT's R-primes) are for residually trivial r̄|G_v, and in that case e does not exist because nothing labels the two eigencharacters. So the one-line proof does not cover the stated generality. Theorem 9.19 uses (1) and (3) directly ("By Lemma 8.2, Spec R^2_∞ is irreducible"). DEFENCE FAILS. (a) The cited [11] = Taylor, Publ. IHES 108 (2008); I fetched it and checked §3. Its setting is 'r̄ : G_{F_v} → {1_n} ⊂ GL_n(k) denote the trivial representation', with #k(v) ≡ 1 mod l. The rings are the literal quotients R^loc_v/I_v^χ. Prop 3.1 concludes: Spec irreducible 'and its generic point has characteristic zero'; R^χ/λ = R^1/λ; components of dimension n^2+1 whose 'generic points all have characteristic zero'. It never states p-torsion-freeness. [76, Lemma 3.3] (BLGHT II, also checked) only concerns completed tensor products: flatness for flat inputs, and minimal primes. Nowhere in §8.5, §8.5.2 or §9.5 is r̄|G_v assumed trivial for v ∈ R. §8.5 explicitly puts the primes where r̄ ramifies into R, and Theorem 5.16(6) allows r̄ to be ramified, or unramified but nontrivial, at such primes. So the hypothesis is not 'clear from context'; the setup contradicts it. COUNTEREXAMPLE (checked): take n = 2, and an extra v ∈ R where r̄ is unramified, r̄(Frob_v) has eigenvalues α ≠ β, and q_v ≡ 1 mod p. By Chebotarev such v exist, and §8.5 allows them. Every lift is γ1 ⊕ ξγ1^{-1}; by Hensel and Nakayama the off-diagonal inertia entries vanish. γ1|I_v factors through the cyclic p-part of k_v^× (order p^a), so u = γ1(t) satisfies u^{p^a} = 1. Lifts split as ρ1 ⊕ ρ2, and ∏_j(ρ2(t) − χ_j(t)) = 0. That gives three disjoint nonempty characteristic-0 loci, so Spec R^χ_x is reducible. sourceIssues.locator: §8.5 (Deformations of Galois representations), published p. 407 (PDF p. 111), 4th line of the page, right after the two bullets defining ξ. arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2, §8.5, PDF p. 81) has the same sentence word for word. arXiv v1 has no n-dimensional §8.5, so the sentence does not appear there.
sourceIssues.printed: [p. 406, end:] "We also fix a continuous character ξ : G_F → O^×" [p. 407, top:] "lifting det(r̄) and with • ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for all v|p, and • ξ|_{I_v} = 1 for all v ∤ p. For example, we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}."
sourceIssues.correction: Minimal fix: "For example, if det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} (as under Theorem 5.16(7)), we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}." General choice: ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}·[χ̄], where χ̄ := det(r̄)·ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} and [·] is the Teichmüller lift into W(k)^× ⊂ O^×. This works because χ̄ is unramified at every finite place. At v|p, Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] makes det(r̄)|_{I_v} = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}|_{I_v}, which is the convention the paper's own bullet ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} presupposes. At v∤p, unipotent ramification makes det(r̄)|_{I_v} = 1. So [χ̄] is unramified at all finite places, and ξ lifts det(r̄) and meets both inertia conditions. The correction proposed in the candidate is therefore correct.
sourceIssues.reason:
I rendered p. 407 and read the text there; it matches arXiv v2 exactly. The §8.5 hypotheses on r̄ are: absolutely irreducible; Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] at v|p; at worst unipotent ramification at v∤p, with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p where r̄ ramifies; odd at the real places. None of these fixes det(r̄). They only force det(r̄)|_{I_v} to be ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} at v|p and trivial at v∤p. So det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}·χ̄, where χ̄ is unramified at every finite place, and χ̄ need not be trivial.

The hypotheses are unchanged by twisting with an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× (whose order is automatically prime to p):
- Fontaine–Laffaille-ness and the weights survive an unramified twist.
- r̄|_{I_v} is unchanged, so unipotence holds and the set of ramified primes is the same.
- At a real place, Trace(c_v) only changes by the sign η(c_v) = ±1, so it stays in {−1,0,1}.
- Absolute irreducibility is preserved.
But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n.

Concrete instance: F = Q(√−47) (class number 5), n = 2, p = 3, r̄ = E[3]|_{G_F} with E = 11a1.
- 3 splits in F, so it is unramified.
- E has good reduction at 3, which gives Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0,1] ⊂ [0,p−2].
- E has split multiplicative reduction at 11 with ord_11(Δ) = 5, so r̄ is unipotently ramified at 11. Also 11 is inert in F (since (−47/11) = −1), so N(v) = 121 ≡ 1 mod 3.
- r̄ is irreducible: 2 splits in F, and Frob_2 has characteristic polynomial X²−X−1, which is irreducible mod 3. (Absolute irreducibility follows from Serre's result that ρ_ℓ is surjective for 11a1 when ℓ ≠ 5. I did not recheck that here.)
- det r̄ = ω, the mod-3 cyclotomic character.
Now twist by a character η of order 5 of the class group, with values in F_81. Then r̄⊗η satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis, and det = ω·η² ≠ ω. So ξ = ε does not reduce to det(r̄⊗η), and the "for example" fails.

I call this an error with no downstream effect. A suitable ξ always exists (the Teichmüller-twisted choice above). The paper only applies §8.5 when det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}: Theorem 5.16(7) assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, and §9.5 assumes r̄ ≅ r̄_m for PGL_n cohomology. So in that setting the example is valid and the results are untouched. The slip is the missing hypothesis in a general setup that deliberately allows any ξ lifting det(r̄). I looked for a defence and found none that covers §8.5 as stated. §8.5 assumes only: absolute irreducibility, Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0..n−1] at v|p, at most unipotent ramification (with N(v) ≡ 1 mod p if ramified) at v∤p, and oddness at real places. Nothing in §8 (§§8.1–8.4 included) fixes det(r̄). Those hypotheses force only that χ̄ = det(r̄)ε̄^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, and such a χ̄ can be nontrivial when F has nontrivial narrow class group.

Explicit failure: take any r̄ satisfying §8.5 and an everywhere-unramified character η: G_F → k^× with η^n ≠ 1 (order necessarily prime to p). Then r̄⊗η still satisfies every §8.5 hypothesis. The unramified twist keeps it Fontaine–Laffaille with the same weights and keeps the ramification unipotent on the same primes. Trace(c_v) only changes sign, so it stays in {−1,0,1}. Irreducibility is kept. But det(r̄⊗η) = det(r̄)·η^n, so det(r̄) and det(r̄⊗η) cannot both equal ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}. For n odd, a character that is unramified at all finite places but nontrivial at a real place already works. The claim does hold automatically over F = Q, where such a χ̄ must be trivial, but the paper allows an arbitrary number field F.

So "we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}" is false as stated: that ξ meets both inertia conditions but need not lift det(r̄).

Why it is harmless: §8.5.1 and §8.5.2 (R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v}, the data S_Q) and Conjecture B / Theorem 9.19 all use only "a fixed ξ with the listed properties", never the specific example. The only route to a stated result is Theorem 5.16 ("follows immediately from Theorem 9.19"). There hypothesis (7) says det(r) = ε^{n(n−1)/2}, so det(r̄) = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2} and the example choice is valid. The PGL(n) automorphic side (§9, G = Res PGL(n)) also forces the determinant of r_m to be a fixed cyclotomic power, so in the application ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is the choice actually needed.

In short, this is an illustrative remark with a missing hypothesis. It is false in the generality of §8.5, but the mathematics is right as intended and in every place it is used.

The 2022 Correction deals only with the brackets and does not touch this passage.
sourceIssues.printed: (p. 407) "Let Q denote a finite set of primes of F disjoint from R ∪ S_p. ... In what follows, R will consist of primes away from p where we allow ramification and Q will consist of Taylor–Wiles primes." (p. 408) "For each v ∈ Q, we assume that: • r̄|_{G_v} ≅ s̄_v ⊕ ψ̄_v where ψ̄_v is a generalized eigenspace of Frobenius of dimension 1. Moreover, we let D_v denote the deformation problem ... consisting of lifts r of r̄|_{G_v} of determinant ξ and of the form ρ ≅ s_v ⊕ ψ_v where s_v (resp. ψ_v) lifts s̄_v (resp. ψ̄_v) and I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars on s_v and ψ_v. Let L_v ⊂ H^1(G_v, ad^0(r̄)) denote the Selmer condition determined by all deformations of r̄|G_v to k[ε]/ε^2 of type D_v. Then dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0(r̄)) = 1."
sourceIssues.correction: Add N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p to the hypotheses on v ∈ Q in §8.5.1. Equivalently, state that dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄) = 1 when N(v) ≡ 1 mod p and = 0 otherwise. This is the smallest fix that makes the statement correct. The candidate's correction is right. Its remark that the equality is used only for the Q given by Prop. 8.5(3) is also right.
sourceIssues.reason:
The statement is false under the hypotheses as printed. Let v ∈ Q and q = N(v). Then v ∤ p and r̄ is unramified at v, because R contains every prime where r̄ ramifies and Q is disjoint from R. Take a lift ρ to k[ε] of type D_v. Wild inertia is pro-ℓ, so its image in the p-group ker(GL_n(k[ε]) → GL_n(k)) is trivial, and ρ|I_v factors through the Z_p(1) quotient of tame inertia. Let σ be a generator there. Then ρ(σ) = diag((1+εa)·1_{s}, (1+εb)·1_{ψ}) with (n−1)a + b = 0, because det = ξ is unramified at v. Since ρ(σ) is block-scalar it commutes with ρ(Frob_v), so the relation Frob σ Frob^{-1} = σ^q forces (q−1)a = 0 in k.

Case q ≢ 1 mod p: then a = b = 0, so every lift of type D_v is unramified. Conversely every unramified lift is of type D_v, because the 1-dimensional generalized eigenspace lifts by Hensel's lemma. Hence L_v = H^1_ur(G_v, ad^0 r̄), and for the procyclic quotient G_v/I_v, dim H^1_ur = h^0. So the difference is 0, not 1. Check with n = 2: let Frobenius have eigenvalues α ≠ β and suppose q ≢ 1 mod p. Then h^0 = 1. Also Hom(G_v, k) = Hom(F_v^×, k) has no ramified part, because k_v^× ⊗ F_p = 0. So L_v = H^1_ur has dimension 1 and the difference is 0.

Case q ≡ 1 mod p: the framed tangent space with fixed determinant has dimension (n^2−1) + 1 = n^2. It equals dim L_v + (n^2 − 1 − h^0), so dim L_v − h^0 = 1, as the paper claims.

Defence considered: the sentence "Q will consist of Taylor–Wiles primes" and the heuristic of §8.2, where a Taylor–Wiles prime has N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^n, show what the authors meant. Against this, the formal hypotheses in §8.5.1 ("Let Q denote a finite set of primes ... disjoint from R ∪ S_p"; "For each v ∈ Q, we assume that: •...") leave the congruence out. Prop. 8.5 then lists "(3) N_{F/Q}(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N" as a separate property, so the paper itself does not treat the congruence as automatic. The analogous passages in §3 and §5 do state "Suppose that x ≡ 1 mod p". So the printed claim is a genuinely missing hypothesis. The meaning is recoverable from context, which puts it on the border between error and misprint.

Consequences: Prop. 8.4 is stated for general Q and keeps the term Σ_{v∈Q}(dim L_v − h^0) unevaluated, so it does not use the claim. The only use is the last line of the proof of Prop. 8.5: "the fact that dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄) = 1 if v ∈ Q". There Q satisfies (3), N(v) ≡ 1 mod p^N, so the equality holds. The exact sequence with the map φ ↦ tr(e_v φ(Frob_v)) in the same proof also relies on (3). The later uses (§9.4.2, §10, the condition "r_m|G_v is of type D_v") involve only Taylor–Wiles sets Q_N from Prop. 8.5. No stated result is affected.

sourceIssues.reason: Only the ℒ(Q)-groups are defined (p. 409). Prop. 8.4 is about R^{□_T}_{𝒮_Q}, and its formula (2) contains Σ_{v∈Q}(dim_k L_v − h^0(G_v, ad^0 r̄)), which is the Euler-characteristic contribution of the Selmer conditions L_v at v ∈ Q. With the Q = ∅ group (classes over G_{F,S}) formula (2) would be false for Q ≠ ∅. The paper itself uses the bare subscript for the Q = ∅ group: Prop. 8.5 asks for q ≥ h^1_{ℒ^⊥,T}, and its proof puts H^1_{ℒ(Q)^⊥,T} and H^1_{ℒ^⊥,T} side by side in one exact sequence. That proof then applies Prop. 8.4 with the Q-groups (using H^1_{ℒ(Q)^⊥,T} = 0 and dim_k L_v − h^0 = 1 for v ∈ Q) to get Prop. 8.5(4). So the intended reading is clear and the argument goes through with it. It is a dropped '(Q)', not a bracket error.

The paper allows K = K_Q or K = L_Q. When K = K_Q the two groups are the same. When K = L_Q, the corestriction H(Y(K)) → H(Y(K')) only makes sense if K' ⊂ K. Also, right multiplication by g sends level H to level g^{−1}Hg. For H = gKg^{−1} ∩ K_Q that level is K ∩ g^{−1}K_Q g, not the printed K ∩ g^{−1}Kg. For the composition to hold together, H has to be gKg^{−1} ∩ K. I checked by hand that the printed group can fail to lie in L_Q. Take v ∈ Q and let g_v be the permutation matrix w that swaps e1 and e2. Take x ∈ L_{Q,v} with x ≡ (a 0 *; 0 b *; 0 0 C) mod π_v, normalised so that b·det C/a^{n−1} ≡ 1. Then wxw^{−1} lies in K_{Q,v}, and the character K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^× takes the value a·det C/b^{n−1} = (a/b)^n on it, which need not be 1. So in general the printed group is not a subgroup of K = L_Q, and the printed diagram does not make sense. This is a genuine inconsistency and not one of the 47 known ⟦ ⟧ bracket errors. It is harmless, though. At places outside Q, K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v}. For the diagonal g actually used (g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) for T_{α,k} and for the T_α at places in Q in Def. 9.1), conjugating by g leaves the (1,1) entry and the determinant of the lower (n−1)×(n−1) block unchanged. So gL_Qg^{−1} ∩ K_Q already lies in L_Q, and the printed and corrected groups coincide. The candidate's reason is correct in substance, though loosely worded.

It affects nothing: nothing later in §9 refers back to the level at p or uses N in this role, and all subsequent statements (Conjecture B, the Hecke algebra definitions, the patching argument) are correct under the evident intended definition. sourceIssues.reason:
Sect. 8.5 (p. 409) defines S_p as the set of primes of F above p, R as disjoint from S_p, and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p. It sets S = S_p ⊔ R and S_Q = S ⊔ Q, and §9 says this notation carries over. In §9.1, conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) covers v ∉ S_Q. So a prime v | p (v ∈ S_p) falls under none of the four conditions, and K_{Q,v}, L_{Q,v} are never defined there. The definitions of K_Q, L_Q, and therefore of Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q), Y_1(Q), are incomplete as printed.

I searched the rest of §9 (Hecke operators, Conjecture B, Lemma 9.6, §9.4–9.5, Thm 9.16, Thm 9.19) and none of it fixes the level at p. By contrast, §5.2.1(4) on p. 330 does state the level at v | p explicitly for the GL_2 case.

The intended meaning is clear from context:
- p > n and p is unramified in F, so PGL_n(O_v) is hyperspecial.
- Conjecture B(1) and the local rings R_v are Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0, …, n−1], i.e. crystalline of trivial weight, which matches hyperspecial (spherical) level at p.
- The coefficients are trivial (O or O(ψ), with ψ supported on R).

So "v ∉ S_Q" is a slip for "v ∉ R ∪ Q". This is a misprint rather than a gap: it is an incomplete definition, not an unproved step. The minor typography on the same page (the missing comma after S_Q, "GL_{N−1}" in (2), "PGL(O_v)" in (1)) is separate and not part of this candidate. None of this is one of the 47 bracket errors. As printed, a place v | p is covered by none of the four conditions. §8.5 defines R as a finite set of primes "disjoint from S_p" and Q as disjoint from R ∪ S_p, so S_Q = S_p ⊔ R ⊔ Q. Conditions (1) and (2) cover v ∈ Q, (4) covers v ∈ R, and (3) excludes every v ∈ S_Q, including S_p. So the factor K_{Q,v} = L_{Q,v} at v | p is never specified, yet Y = Y(K_∅), Y_0(Q) and Y_1(Q) all need it.

Defence attempts that fail:
(a) §9 cannot be using a different S_Q. The §9 preamble explicitly takes S_Q = S_p ∪ R ∪ Q from §8, and Definition 9.1 uses "α which are units at primes in S_Q", which excludes the Hecke operators at p. That only makes sense if S_Q contains S_p.
(b) Reading "such that" as allowing any level at p does not rescue the text. Conjecture B(1) asserts that r_m|G_v is Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1] for v | p. At deeper level at p, for example Iwahori, the Hecke algebra would also see semistable, non-crystalline lifts, and (1) would fail. The patching in Theorem 9.19 likewise uses the Fontaine–Laffaille rings R_v of Lemma 8.2 at v | p.
(c) No later passage in §9 fixes the level at p. Lemma 9.6 talks only of "congruence subgroups commensurable with PGL2(O_F)", and §9.5 just uses Y = Y(K_∅).

The intended level (hyperspecial at p) is clear from context:
- Conjecture B(1).
- Theorem 5.16: (1)–(2) crystalline with Hodge–Tate weights 0,…,n−1 and p unramified in F; (8a) "good reduction at all v | p"; (8b) Serre-modular of minimal level N(r̄), which is prime to p.
- The parallel published §5.2.1(3)–(4) and arXiv v1 §4.2.1, which both give the level at v | p explicitly. Presumably the p-clause was lost when that template was rewritten as the S_Q-based (3).

sourceIssues.reason: R ⊂ S_Q. The construction of T(g) on p. 412 is stated only for g trivial at each v ∈ R. That restriction is needed because on the ψ-twisted local system the operator depends on the representative g, not just the double coset. If α_v ∈ 𝒪_v^× with α_v ≠ 1 at some v ∈ R, then g_v = diag(α_v, ..., α_v, 1, ..., 1) is a non-trivial element of Iw(v), and it maps non-trivially to Iw(v)/Iw_1(v) ≅ (k_v^×)^n/k_v^×. So T_{α,k} is not covered by the stated construction, and Definition 9.1 as printed refers to operators the paper has not defined. The mismatch is harmless. With the natural extension (right translation by g_v is a deck transformation of Ỹ → Y and acts on 𝒪(ψ) by ψ_v(g_v)^{±1}), such a T_{α,k} is a unit scalar in 1 + 𝔪_𝒪 times T_{α',k}, where α' has v-component 1. So the 𝒪-algebra generated is unchanged. At v|p a unit α_v gives g_v ∈ PGL_n(𝒪_v), which is harmless. At v ∈ Q a unit α_v gives the diamond operators through K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×. The printed 'units' includes these deliberately or not; the minimal correction keeps them, as printed. Whether they should be in T^an is the separate gap about local–global compatibility at Q, and it does not affect this verdict. It is not a bracket error.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked this against the page images (PDF pp. 116–118 = pp. 412–414) and the text. It holds.
(1) §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,k} is the double coset operator for g = diag(α,…,α,1,…,1) with k copies of α, and k = n is allowed (Definition 9.1). For k = n, g is scalar, so it is the identity in PGL_n and T_{α,n} = id. Under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term (−1)^n N^{n(n−1)/2} T_{λ,n} then gives det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n}.
(2) Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius (Notation, p. 306), so det r̄_𝔪 = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2−n} by Chebotarev.
(3) §8.5 fixes r̄ as Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1]. It also fixes ξ lifting det r̄, with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v|p and ξ|I_v = 1 for v∤p. Theorem 5.16(7) has det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. Conjecture B supposes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄ and concludes that r_𝔪 is a deformation of type S_Q, so it has determinant ξ. §9.5 assumes a maximal ideal 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Together these force ω^{−n} = 1 on I_v for v|p. Since p is unramified in F, that means (p−1) | n. With p > n this happens only when p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2, the printed Conjecture B, part 1, rules out every 𝔪 with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄.
(4) Independent check. The un-normalised T_{α,k} acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I verified numerically that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So without the factor, the formula gives 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, which has weights 0,…,n−1 and determinant ε^{n(n−1)/2}, as the paper's conventions require. With the factor, every root is multiplied by N^{−1}, so the formula describes r⊗ε^{−1}. For n = 2 it gives X^2 − (T_α/N)X + N^{−1}, which contradicts Conjecture A for the same T_α. For n ≥ 3 the determinant is wrong whichever sign or Frobenius convention is used. Lemma 9.6 also uses the un-normalised T_x (roots α_x, β_x with α_xβ_x = N(x)).
Two small problems with the candidate's reasoning:
- The mod-𝔪 contradiction needs p ≥ n+2, not just p > n. When p = n+1 one needs 𝔪-adic or characteristic-zero information instead.
- Printed B is not literally self-contradictory. Its part-3 hypothesis (and §9.5's standing assumption) simply cannot be met, so Theorem 9.19 becomes vacuous. The proof of 5.16 also fails: by the standard normalisation, the 𝔪 coming from π_0 would give r̄⊗ε̄^{−1}, not r̄.
Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} in dimension 2n with large p, so it is affected. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. I checked the page images: PDF pp. 115–118, pp. 77–79 and 87–88, and v2 p. 86.

Defences tried, and why each fails:
(a) Is T_{α,n} = id? Yes. §9 takes G = Res_{F/Q}PGL(n) (p. 411), and for k = n the matrix g = diag(α,…,α) is scalar, hence trivial in PGL_n. So under the printed normalisation T_{λ,n} = N(λ)^{−n}. The constant term then says det r̄_𝔪(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2−n} = N(λ)^{n(n−3)/2} for every λ ∉ S_Q. This does not depend on how T_{α,k} is read for k < n: using α^{-1} just swaps T_k with T_{n−k}, and the determinant is unchanged.
(b) Frobenius convention. The Notation on p. 306 says Frob_v is the arithmetic Frobenius. Chebotarev then gives det r̄_𝔪 = ω^{n(n−3)/2}. Using the geometric Frobenius instead gives ε^{−n(n−3)/2}. That agrees with ε^{n(n−1)/2} on inertia only if ε^{n(n−2)} = 1, so it helps only when n = 2. The paper uses the arithmetic Frobenius anyway: Conjecture A has X^2 − T_λX + N(λ), and Lemma 5.6 has cyclotomic determinant.
(c) The paper's own T(g), defined by corestriction, then translation, then pushforward, acts on constant classes by its degree, the q-binomial [n,k]_q. I checked numerically (q = 5, 7, 9; n = 2..5) that q^{i(i−1)/2}[n,i]_q = e_i(1,q,…,q^{n−1}). So the unnormalised operators give 1⊕ε⊕…⊕ε^{n−1}, as intended. The printed normalised operators give roots q^{−1},1,…,q^{n−2}, which is r⊗ε^{−1}. No convention in the paper supplies the factor N^{−k}. Lemma 9.6 itself uses the unnormalised T_x: φ^∨∘φ = [[N(x)+1, T_x],[T_x, N(x)+1]] with α_xβ_x ≡ N(x).

Consequences. Conjecture B assumes r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Here det r̄ = ξ̄ with ξ|I_v = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p, and p is unramified, so ω(I_v) = F_p^×. The printed text would therefore force (p−1) | n, which for p > n means p = n+1. So for p ≥ n+2 no 𝔪 satisfies r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄. Parts (1)–(5) of B become vacuous, and the standing assumption of §9.5 (p. 425, "a maximal ideal 𝔪 of T with r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄") can never hold. When p = n+1, part (1) (Fontaine–Laffaille weights [0..n−1]) fails at any characteristic-0 point instead, because of the ε^{−1} twist.

The deduction "Theorem 5.16 follows immediately from Theorem 9.19" also breaks. The 𝔪 attached to π_0 in hypothesis (8a) would, under the printed normalisation, have r̄_𝔪 ≅ r̄⊗ω^{−1}, not r̄. And with B vacuous, 5.16 would claim far more than is proved. Theorem 1.1 applies 5.16 to Sym^{2n−1} (dimension 2n) at large p, so it inherits the problem.

Unaffected: Conjecture B(5) and Lemma 9.6. They only involve Taylor–Wiles primes, where N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, and the projectors lim Q_x(V_x)^{k!} do not change when V_x is scaled by a unit ≡ 1.

Remark on the kind: the intended normalisation is recoverable from §5, so some would call this a slip. But the printed definition, which introduces a deliberate normalisation, makes the hypothesis of 5.16/9.19 unsatisfiable. The correction is right and minimal. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

sourceIssues.correction:
Add to Conjecture B a local–global compatibility clause at the Taylor–Wiles primes. This is the GL(n) analogue of Conjecture A(3), where T_α uses g = diag(α,1). Proposed clause: for v ∈ Q and α ∈ O_v^×, the operator T_{α,1} acts on H^*_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_𝔪 as the scalar by which r_𝔪(Art_v(α)) acts on the lift ψ_v of the line ψ̄_v. Here Art is normalised as in (3), with the transpose/inverse when one passes to the dual/homology side (𝔪*).

Why this is the right form: identify K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} with k_v^× by g ↦ det(B)·a^{1−n}, where g ≡ [[a,*],[0,B]]. Then diag(α^{(k)},1^{(n−k)}) has class α^{k−n}, and T_{α,1} has class α^{1−n}. Since p > n, the T_{α,1} run over the whole p-part of Δ_Q. So the clause fixes the diamond action of S_N = O[Δ_N]; equivalently, a diamond operator acts by the inertial scalar on s_v. With the clause, R_{𝒮_Q} → T is a map of O[Δ_Q]-algebras. The diamond operators lie in the image of R_{𝒮_Q}, so the p. 415 surjection holds even though T^an contains them. The augmentation ideal maps into the image of ker(R_{𝒮_Q} → R_𝒮), which gives both halves of Theorem 6.3(d). A relation "diamond = inertial character to a fixed power prime to p" would do just as well; this is all that is needed.

Alternative for Definition 9.1: read "units" as "trivial" at Q, as in Def. 5.4. That saves the p. 415 surjection but not (d); the clause is still needed.

Comments on the reporters' versions. X-K10-9's form (T_{α,1} ↔ ψ_v∘Art_v) is correct, but its cross-reference "p. 378" should be pp. 374–375. C-K9-0's phrase "ψ_x∘Art_x ... should match the Hecke action of the T_{α,k}" holds only for k = 1. Under the expected compatibility, T_{α,k} with α ∈ O_v^× acts by (ψ_v∘Art_v)^{(n−k)/(n−1)}, and T_{α,n} = 1. H-part2-18's "diamond character, or its inverse" is right only for a suitable choice of the unspecified isomorphism K_{Q,v}/L_{Q,v} ≅ k_v^×.
sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the printed text on the page images and it matches the quote.

1. What Theorem 6.3(d) asks for (p. 386, checked on the image). "the image of S_M^□ in End_O(H^*(D_M^□ ⊗_{S_M} S_N/ϖ^n)) is contained in the image of R_∞ and moreover, the image of the augmentation ideal of S_N^□ ... is contained in the image of ker(φ_N)." In §9.5, S_N = O[Δ_N] acts through the deck group of Y_{Δ_N}(Q) → Y_0(Q). That group is a quotient of K_Q/L_Q ≅ ∏ k_x^×, so S_N acts by diamond operators. R_∞ acts through R_{S_Q} → Hecke. The map φ_N sends R_∞ onto R_S, and ker(R_{S_Q} → R_S) is generated by the condition that inertia at Q acts trivially.

2. What Conjecture B gives at v ∈ Q. Only (2): r_𝔪|_{G_v} has type 𝒟_v. In §8.5.1 (p. 408), 𝒟_v is purely Galois-theoretic: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars on s_v and ψ_v". Clauses (1) and (3)–(5) are about v|p, v ∈ R, vanishing, and Y_0(Q) respectively. None of them ties the inertial scalars at v ∈ Q to the diamond operators. r_𝔪 is determined by Frobenius at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial character at v is a well-defined object. Saying that this character equals the diamond character is extra local–global content. Without it, nothing stops r_𝔪 from being unramified at v while ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1. The second half of (d) then fails, and so can the first half. Conclusion (iv) of Theorem 6.3, which is used to finish the proof of Thm 9.19, needs the second half.

3. The paper's own GL_2 argument uses exactly this input. Conjecture A(3) (pp. 374–375) is local–global compatibility at Q. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees ... that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380 the authors write: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. The second part of condition (5a) follows from Conjecture A part (3)". Conjecture B has no counterpart to A(3).

4. The claimed surjection R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪}. As printed, Definition 9.1 allows α that are only units at primes in S_Q. For α ∈ O_x^× with x ∈ Q, diag(α^{(k)}, 1^{(n−k)}) lies in K_{Q,x}. By my computation it acts on Y_1(Q) as a diamond operator (class α^{k−n}). So T^an contains the diamond operators, and surjectivity from the trace algebra again needs the missing compatibility. If "units" was meant to be "trivial", as in Def. 5.4, then the first half of (d) needs it instead.

5. Independent corroboration. Khare–Thorne, "Potential automorphy and the Leopoldt conjecture" (arXiv 1409.7007), which uses the Calegari–Geraghty method, builds this into its setup. It defines D_v^TW so that "C_i|_{I_{F_v}} agrees, on composition with the Artin map, with the ith canonical character" of Δ_v, makes R_{S_Q} an O[Δ_Q]-algebra, and puts the requirement in a separate Conjecture 6.27. Its Remark 6.28 calls that conjecture "a form of local-global compatibility ... at the places of S_p ∪ Q".

This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The O[(Z_p)^q] on p. 427 is one of those and is a separate matter.

On "affects": the proof of Theorem 9.19 has a gap. Theorems 5.16 and 1.1 are deduced from it assuming Conjecture B, so their hypothesis must be strengthened by the clause above for the proof to go through. Nothing shows the conditional statements are false, so "the proof" is the right classification. Defence attempts. None of them works.

(a) The other clauses of Conjecture B. Clause (1) concerns v|p. Clause (3) gives inertia compatibility only at v ∈ R, with fixed O-valued Iwahori characters. Clause (4) is about vanishing. Clause (5) concerns only Y_0(Q), where the diamond operators act trivially. Clause (2) says only that the lift has type 𝒟_v, which is a purely Galois-side condition: "I_v acts via (possibly different) scalars" (p. 408). Nothing ties those scalars to the deck group Δ_Q of Y_1(Q) → Y_0(Q). r_𝔪 is pinned down by its Frobenius traces at λ ∉ S_Q, so its inertial scalar at v ∈ Q is a definite object. Saying that it equals the diamond character is an extra assertion, and Conjecture B does not make it. In particular, clauses (1)–(5) do not rule out r_𝔪 being unramified at v while a diamond operator ⟨δ⟩ ≠ 1.

(b) The GL(1) and central-character mechanisms. In the GL(1) model (PDF 108), and for classical X_1(N), diamond operators come from Frobenius classes through class field theory or the central character. Here G = PGL_n, so T_{λ,n} = 1 and det = ξ carries no diamond information. The p-part of Δ_Q is therefore not in the closed algebra generated by traces unless one assumes something more.

(c) A charitable reading of the authors' intent. Remark 9.5 (p. 417) says the real difficulty lies in "proving local-global compatibility, especially at v|p". So the authors think of local–global compatibility as part of the conjecture's content. But the stated clause at Q is only (2). The proof says "Condition (d) follows from Conjecture B" and gives no argument.

(d) Deriving it from clause (3). One could try to treat Q as additional R-primes with character twists and then decompose. That is not in the paper. It would also fail integrally: patching needs O/ϖ^n and O[Δ]-coefficients, where eigen-decomposition by O-valued characters is not available.

(e) The same step in §5. The paper's GL(2) proof needed exactly this input and said so. The proof of Lemma 5.6 says "assumption 3 above guarantees (by Hensel's Lemma) that the T_α for α|Q lie in the O-subalgebra generated by traces". On p. 380: "The image of S_N ... is contained in the image of R_∞ by Conjecture A, because it is given by the image of the diamond operators. The second part of condition (5a) follows from Conjecture A part (3)". Here T_α uses g = diag(α,1) (§5.2.2), which is T_{α,1}. Conjecture B has no counterpart of A(3).

What the gap breaks.
- As printed, Definition 9.1 lets α be units at Q. For α ∈ O_v^×, diag(α^{(k)},1) ∈ K_{Q,v} normalises L_{Q,v}. So T_{α,k} is the deck transformation of class α^{k−n}. T^an_{Q,1} therefore contains the diamond operators, and the p. 415 surjection R_{𝒮_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,𝔪} does not follow for Q ≠ ∅. For Q = ∅ it is fine, and that case is the only one used as a surjection in §9.5 (R_𝒮 ↠ T_𝔪).
- Theorem 6.3(d) (p. 386) has two halves. Both need the compatibility.
  - The first half says the image of S_M lies in the image of R_∞. It is used on p. 388 to make H^*(P_∞) finite over R_∞.
  - The second half says the augmentation ideal maps into the image of ker φ_N. It gives conclusion (iv). The last lines of the proof of Thm 9.19 (p. 428) use (iv) to pass from near-faithfulness of H^{l0}(P_∞) to that of H^{q0}(Y,K/O)^∨_𝔪. Knowing only that ker φ kills H, a quotient of P/𝔞P, is not enough.

Consequences. The proof of Theorem 9.19 is incomplete. Theorem 5.16 is deduced from 9.19 ("follows ... immediately"), and Theorem 1.1 (§10) from 5.16, both under "Assume Conjecture B". Their proofs go through once Conjecture B is strengthened by the clause above. Nothing shows the conditional statements are false, so the affected thing is the proof.

Separate from this candidate: in the same step, condition (b) needs R_{𝒮_Q} to act on the intermediate covers Y_{Δ_N}(Q_M). Conjecture B is stated only for Y_1(Q). This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

I checked the page image. On PDF p. 119, which is published p. 415 (§9.3, the last sentence of the paragraph after Conjecture B), the text reads "for n = 1". A 300 dpi zoom confirms the letter is n. The arXiv v2 text has the same sentence (cg-v2.txt l. 4604-4606), so this is not a typesetting defect and is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

Conjecture B (pp. 414-415) uses its letters consistently. n is the rank: r̄_m : G_F → GL_n(T^an_{Q,ψ}/m), the characteristic polynomial X^n − ..., and condition (1) "weights equal to [0,1,...,n−1]". The coefficient exponent in conditions (4)(a), (4)(b) and (5) is m: H^i_ψ(Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, H^i_ψ(∂Y_1(Q), O/ϖ^m)_m, and H^*_ψ(Y, O/ϖ^m)_m → H^*_ψ(Y_0(Q), O/ϖ^m)_{m_Q}. Read literally, "n = 1" would mean GL_1, which makes no sense here. The phrase "with coefficients in the residue field k = O/ϖ" shows the exponent 1 is intended.

Elsewhere the paper sometimes uses n as a coefficient exponent too. For example, the proof of Lemma 9.6 on p. 416 uses O/ϖ^n while n = 2 is the rank. So the letters are loose in places, but the sentence explicitly refers to conditions 4 and 5, which are written with ϖ^m.

I redid the dévissage myself, and the claim is correct with m. Take the exact sequences 0 → O/ϖ^{m−1} → O/ϖ^m → O/ϖ → 0, where the first map is multiplication by ϖ. The long exact sequences in cohomology are Hecke-equivariant, and localization at m is exact. So by induction, vanishing for m = 1 gives vanishing for all m in (4)(a) and (4)(b). For (5), the maps lim_k ∏ Q_x(V_x)^{k!} come from Hecke operators on complexes, so they commute with the connecting maps. The five lemma then carries the m = 1 isomorphism to all m. The converse direction is trivial.

The candidate's correction and reason are accurate.

By §8.4's formulas, GL(2) over a CM quartic field (r2 = 2) has l0 = 2 and d = 6, so q0 = 2. GL(3)/Q has l0 = 1 and d = 5, so q0 = 2. In both cases H^{q0−1} = H^1. Poincaré/Verdier duality (see the paper's own use of it in §9 and Remark 9.5) pairs H^i(Y,k)_{𝔪^*} with H_c^{d−i}(Y,k)_𝔪. So "by duality, considering both 𝔪 and 𝔪^*" turns the vanishing of H^1 given by the congruence subgroup property into the vanishing of H_c^{d−1}, not H_c^{q0−1} = H_c^1. The next sentence ("the vanishing of H_c^{q0−1} implies the vanishing of H^{q0−1}", because the boundary cohomology vanishes at 𝔪) is then circular as printed: H^{q0−1} = H^1 is exactly what the congruence subgroup property already gave.

The degree that actually needs this argument is never treated. For GL(2) over a CM quartic field, the range is [2,4] and d = 6. H^0_𝔪 = 0 because 𝔪 is non-Eisenstein. H^6 = 0 by virtual cohomological dimension: vcd = d − (Q-rank) = 6 − 1 = 5. But H^5 is not automatic, and it needs exactly the duality step with degree d−1 = 5 = q0+l0+1. For GL(3)/Q, vcd = 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 happens to vanish anyway, but the argument as intended still concerns degree d−1 = 4. With the correction, the remark reads coherently: H^1_𝔪 = 0 (congruence subgroup property), so H_c^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (duality over 𝔪 and 𝔪^*), so H^{d−1}_𝔪 = 0 (boundary vanishing at 𝔪).

Each printed sentence is literally true: H_c^1_𝔪 ≅ H^1_𝔪 = 0 via the boundary sequence. The fault is the index, which makes the duality step misattributed and leaves the top degree out. The intended meaning (the Poincaré-dual degree of 1) is clear from "by duality", so I class it as an index misprint; "error" is also defensible, since the printed step fails to cover degree d−1. It sits in a remark supporting a conjecture, so nothing proved in the paper depends on it. This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. The paper sets up Y(K) for G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) in §9, and §8.4 says dim Y = 2q_0+l_0. For GL(2) over a quartic CM field (r_2 = 2) this gives l_0 = 2 and d = 6. For GL(3)/Q it gives l_0 = 1 and d = 5. So q_0 = 2 in both cases, as the remark says.

Part (4)(a) needs the localized cohomology to vanish outside [q_0, q_0+l_0]:
- GL(2)/F: degrees 0, 1, 5 and 6.
- GL(3)/Q: degrees 0, 1, 4 and 5.

H^0_m = 0 because m is non-Eisenstein. H^d = 0 because Y is non-compact. The congruence subgroup property gives H^1_m = 0 for every non-Eisenstein m, including m^*.

Poincaré duality is Hecke-equivariant up to replacing m by m^*: (H_c^{d−i})_m is dual to (H^i)_{m^*}. That is why the text says "considering both m and m^*". So from H^1 it gives vanishing of H_c^{d−1} = H_c^{q_0+l_0+1}, not of H_c^{q_0−1} = H_c^1. The boundary sequence then turns this into (H^{d−1})_m = 0.

As printed, q_0−1 = 1, so the remark fails in two ways:
- Duality is credited with giving H_c^1. H_c^1 does vanish, but through the boundary sequence, not through duality.
- The next sentence concludes (H^1)_m = 0, which was the starting point, so it is circular.
- Degree d−1 is never treated. This matters for GL(2)/F: the virtual cohomological dimension is 6 − 1 = 5 = d−1, so H^5 does not vanish for free. (For GL(3)/Q it is 5 − 2 = 3, so H^4 would vanish anyway.)

Defence considered: no convention in the paper shifts the indexing of H_c. Remark 9.5 uses the same duality, which reverses degrees between cohomology and compactly supported cohomology. No reading makes "q_0−1" the degree that duality produces. The only intended degree consistent with the words "by duality, m and m^*" and with the goal of (4)(a) is d−1 = q_0+l_0+1. The intended meaning is therefore clear from context. It is a wrong-index slip, the protocol's example of a misprint. It could also be called an error with affects = nothing, since the argument as printed does not close; the candidate chose that.

Consequences: Remark 9.3 is cited nowhere else in the paper. The §9 results (Theorem 9.19 etc.) assume Conjecture B outright. The later Ihara-type argument uses the congruence subgroup property of the S-arithmetic group PSL_2(O_F[1/x]) on its own, not this remark. The remark's claim, that (4)(a) can be checked in these cases, is true once the degree is corrected.

sourceIssues.locator: §9 (Conjecture B discussion), Remark 9.3, published p. 415 (PDF p. 119). arXiv v2 (1207.4224v2) has identical text, citing [BMS67]. arXiv v1 ("... I") has no such remark. Serre's 1970 SL_2 paper is not in the bibliography of either version; the only other Serre item nearby is [78], Arbres, amalgames, SL_2.
sourceIssues.printed: Remark 9.3 Part (4)(a) of Conjecture B may be verified directly in a number of small rank cases, in particular for GL(2)/F when F is CM field of degree either 2 or 4, or for GL(3)/Q. In the latter two cases (where (q_0, l_0) = (2, 2) and (2, 1) respectively), the key point is that the lattices in question satisfy the congruence subgroup property [77], which yields vanishing for both (H^1)_m and (by duality, considering both m and m^*) (H_c^{q_0-1})_m where m is a non-Eisenstein maximal ideal. [Bibliography] 77. Bass, H., Milnor, J., Serre, J.-P.: Solution of the congruence subgroup problem for SL_n (n ≥ 3) and Sp_2n (n ≥ 2). Inst. Hautes Études Sci. Publ. Math. 33, 59–137 (1967)
sourceIssues.correction: Cite Serre's paper as well: J.-P. Serre, "Le problème des groupes de congruence pour SL2", Ann. of Math. (2) 92 (1970), 489–527. Suggested wording: "...satisfy the congruence subgroup property ([77] for GL(3)/Q; Serre, Ann. of Math. 92 (1970) for GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4)". Serre proves that the congruence kernel of SL2(O_S) is finite when |S| ≥ 2, that is, when O_F^× is infinite. For a CM quartic field the unit rank is r1+r2−1 = 1, so this applies. For a totally imaginary F the kernel is μ(F), which is finite but not trivial. So "congruence subgroup property" here has to mean a finite kernel. The proposed correction is right and minimal.
sourceIssues.reason: I rendered PDF p. 119 and read the text: "the latter two cases" are GL(2)/F with F CM of degree 4 ((q_0,l_0)=(2,2)) and GL(3)/Q ((2,1)), and the paper cites only [77] for both. [77] is Bass–Milnor–Serre, whose title and content restrict it to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. Since Sp_2 = SL_2 is excluded, SL_2 is not covered. For the GL(2)/F case the lattice sits in G = SL_2 over F (the restriction of scalars of SL_2 from F), and no isogeny turns this into SL_n with n ≥ 3 or Sp_2n with n ≥ 2. I checked the attribution in the survey by Prasad–Rapinchuk, "Developments on the congruence subgroup problem after the work of Bass, Milnor and Serre" (arXiv:0809.1622), §2.3: "The results obtained in [3] exhibited two possibilities for C^S(G) for G = SL_n (n ⩾ 3) and Sp_2n (n ⩾ 2) ... Subsequently, it was shown in [49] that this description of C^S(G) remains valid for G = SL_2 if |S| > 1." Here [3] is BMS and [49] is Serre 1970. §5.6 of the same survey calls the SL_2 case with |S| > 1 "established first by Serre in [49]". BMS §15 only states the metaplectic conjecture for SL_2. For F a CM quartic field, S is the set of archimedean places, which are 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and Dirichlet gives unit rank 1. Serre's theorem therefore applies and gives C ≅ μ_F. The mathematical claim in the remark is true, but the reference given does not prove it for one of the two cases it is cited for. That is an asserted step without adequate support, i.e. a citation gap. It sits in a heuristic remark and the statement is true, so nothing downstream is affected. The case for the paper is only partly sound. For GL(3)/Q the lattices are commensurable with SL3(Z), and [77] proves a trivial congruence kernel there, so the citation fits. For GL(2)/F with F a quartic CM field, the lattices are commensurable with SL2(O_F), or equivalently with arithmetic subgroups of SL2(C)^2. [77] cannot cover them. Its title and theorems are limited to SL_n with n ≥ 3 and Sp_2n with n ≥ 2, which excludes Sp_2 = SL2. The SL2 case was left open there and settled later by Serre (Ann. Math. 1970), who showed the kernel is finite exactly when |S| ≥ 2. The fact the remark asserts is true: F has 2 complex places, so |S| = 2 and CSP holds with kernel μ(F). The imaginary-quadratic case is correctly left out of "the latter two cases", since |S| = 1 there and CSP fails. So the mathematics is right, but half of its stated justification is missing. This matches the repo's precedent of recording a missing or wrong citation as "gap / nothing". It is not one of the 47 bracket errors. Consequences: [77] is used only in this remark, nothing in the paper refers back to Remark 9.3, and the remark is a side comment on how plausible Conjecture B is. All later results in §9 assume Conjecture B as a hypothesis. Side note, not verified: for totally imaginary F the kernel μ(F) is nontrivial, so the "yields vanishing of (H^1)_m" step may need extra care when p divides |μ(F)|. The remark is informal ("may be verified directly"), and this candidate does not claim that.

sourceIssues.reason:
I checked the rendered pages 407, 408, 412, 413, 414 and 415.
(i) In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 412). So g = diag(α,…,α) is trivial in G(A^∞), and T_{α,n} = T(1) = id. The normalised T_{λ,n} is therefore a scalar: N(λ)^{−n} as printed, or 1 with the §5 normalisation. The constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B then makes det r_m(Frob_λ) a fixed power of N(λ). By Chebotarev, det r_m = ε^k with k fixed; k = n(n−1)/2 once the normalisation is repaired (X-K9-0, a separate issue).
(ii) Type S_Q requires "(2) it is of determinant ξ" (§8.5.2, p. 408). The local rings R_v, R_v^1, R_v^{χ_v} and D_v also fix the determinant as ξ.
(iii) §8.5 (p. 407) fixes ξ only as a continuous lift of det r̄ with ξ|_{I_v} = ε^{n(n−1)/2} for v | p and ξ|_{I_v} = 1 for v ∤ p. It then says "For example, we can simply take ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}". Nothing in §9 or §9.5 specialises ξ; the only occurrences of ξ are in §8.5. So θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place, hence a character of the narrow class group, and θ ≡ 1 mod m. It can be non-trivial.
Concrete admissible data: F = Q(√−23) (h = 3), p = 3 > n = 2, where 3 is unramified and split, and O = Z_3[ζ_3]. Take θ a non-trivial character Cl(F) → μ_3 and ξ = εθ. This satisfies every condition of §8.5. Then det r_m = ε ≠ εθ = ξ in T_m^× whenever θ is non-trivial in T_m, for example when m supports characteristic-0 cohomology, as with π_0 in Theorem 5.16(8a). In that case r_m is not of type S_Q, so "It follows" fails.
The fix is harmless. Theorem 5.16(7) forces ξ = det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} when Theorem 9.19 is applied. Alternatively, twisting by η restores a type-S_Q lift, and the surjection survives because the η(Frob_λ) are units.
This is not one of the 47 bracket errors. It is also distinct from X-K9-0: after that correction the issue remains unless ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. As an alternative classification, this is a missing hypothesis, which could be recorded as a gap. I checked all three passages against the page images (PDF pp. 111, 112, 118, 119).

(1) What the determinant of r_m is. In §9, G = Res_{F/Q} PGL(n) (p. 411). T_{α,n} is the Hecke operator for diag(α,…,α), which is trivial in PGL_n, so T_{α,n} = id. With the unnormalised operators, the constant term of the characteristic polynomial in Conjecture B gives det r_m(Frob_λ) = N(λ)^{n(n−1)/2} for all λ ∉ S_Q. Chebotarev then gives det r_m = ε^{n(n−1)/2}. This uses the correction of X-K9-0 / H-part2-17. With the printed 1/N(a)^k normalisation one gets ε^{n(n−3)/2}, which is a separate error. Either way, det r_m is a fixed power of ε and has nothing to do with ξ.

(2) What type S_Q requires. It requires det = ξ (condition (2), p. 408). §8.5 allows any ξ lifting det r̄ with the stated restrictions on inertia. Since r̄_m ≅ r̄ gives det r̄ = ε̄^{n(n−1)/2}, the character θ = ξε^{−n(n−1)/2} is unramified at every finite place and trivial mod m_O. It is also trivial at real places, because p is odd. So θ is a character of Cl_F of p-power order. It can be non-trivial whenever p | h_F and ζ_p ∈ O. The paper forces ζ_p ∈ O as soon as R ≠ ∅, since the distinct χ_{v,i}/ψ_v factor through (k_v^×)^n/k_v^× into 1+m_O. Example: F = Q(√−23), h_F = 3, p = 3 > n = 2, 3 splits in F, O ∋ ζ_3, θ : Cl_F ↠ μ_3, ξ = εθ. Every §8.5 condition holds, but det r_m = ε ≠ ξ. So "It follows that r_m is of type S_Q" fails for this choice of ξ. If p ∤ h_F, ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} is forced and the sentence is correct. Nothing in §9 fixes ξ.

(3) The defence, and why nothing downstream breaks. θ has p-power order and p > n, so θ^{1/n} exists, is unramified everywhere and is ≡ 1 mod m_O. The twist r_m ⊗ θ^{1/n} reduces to r̄ and has det ξ. At v|p it is still Fontaine–Laffaille with weights [0,…,n−1], since the twist is unramified and within the FL range. At v ∈ R its inertial characteristic polynomials are unchanged. At v ∈ Q it is still of type D_v. So it is of type S_Q (resp. S_Q^χ). Its trace algebra equals that of r_m, because tr(r_m⊗θ^{1/n})(g) = θ^{1/n}(g)·tr r_m(g) with θ^{1/n}(g) ∈ O^×. So R_{S_Q} ↠ T^an_{Q,1,m} still exists.

Where the sentence is used:
- §9.5, p. 426: "By Conjecture B, we have surjections R_S ↠ T_m and R_{S^χ} ↠ T_{χ,m}".
- Theorem 9.19 and its proof, p. 427, where R_{S_{Q_N}} acts on cohomology "by Conjecture B".
All of these survive if one uses the same fixed twist for every N and for both the 1- and χ-versions; the twist also commutes with the diamond and inertia data at Q. Theorem 5.16 assumes det r = ε^{n(n−1)/2} (hypothesis (7)), and r must be of type S, so ξ = ε^{n(n−1)/2} there and the printed sentence is literally correct. Theorem 1.1 goes through 5.16.

So the paper's text is a genuine, harmless slip: the asserted step fails for some ξ that §8.5 allows. The candidate labels it a gap; 'error' fits PROTOCOL §18 slightly better, because the step is false rather than merely unproved. It is not one of the 47 bracket errors.

If the eigenvalues of ρ̄(Frob_x) are α_x and β_x, then α_x β_x ≡ N(x) ≡ 1 mod p. [...] It follows that T_x^2 − (1 + N(x))^2 ∉ 𝔪, and hence φ^∨ ∘ φ is invertible after localizing at 𝔪." sourceIssues.correction: The determinant of the printed matrix is (N(x)+1)^2 − T_x^2, which is −(T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2). The follow-on sentence "T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2 ∉ 𝔪" is still correct as written, because it is the same element up to a sign.
sourceIssues.reason: I recomputed it: det[[a,b],[b,a]] = a^2 − b^2. With a = N(x)+1 and b = T_x this gives (1+N(x))^2 − T_x^2. The paper prints T_x^2 − (1+N(x))^2, which is the negative, so this is a real sign slip. The matrix is taken exactly as printed, so no convention in the paper makes the stated sign right. The expression is used only once afterwards, to say it is not in 𝔪, and so φ^∨∘φ is invertible after localizing. That property does not depend on the sign. Mod 𝔪 we have T_x ≡ α+β and N(x) ≡ αβ ≡ 1, so the expression reduces to ±(1−α)(1−β)(1+α)(1+β). This is nonzero exactly when α, β ≢ ±1, which is the Taylor–Wiles condition. A search of the text finds the expression nowhere else. The 47 known bracket errors are unrelated. Minor note: the candidate's "printed" field writes the determinant as "T_x^2 − (1 + N(x))^2", which matches the page.

sourceIssues.printed: p. 417: "For convenience, let us also assume that x is trivial in the ray class group corresponding to the component group of Y (this is equivalent to imposing a further congruence condition on x, but is imposed only for notational convenience in the argument below). ... (Without the extra assumption on x, one would have to amalgamate different pairs of lattices Γ_i occurring in the decomposition of Y according to the action of the ray class group, cf. Sect. 4.1.4 of [6]. The argument would then proceed quite similarly, but it would require more notation)". p. 418: "We claim that this sequence is equivariant with respect to the Hecke operator U_{x^2}, which acts on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) by 1. First, recall the definition of U_{x^2}. It is defined to be 1/N(x)^2 times the operator induced by taking the double coset operator for Γ^1_0(x) corresponding to the matrix: (π_x^2 0; 0 1). ... g := (π_x 0; 0 π_x^{-1}). With this normalization, the matrix g lies in G. In particular, the corresponding map on H^*(G, O/ϖ^n) is given by multiplication by the degree of this operator on Γ^1_0(x), which is N(x)^2, and thus (after normalizing) it follows that U_{x^2} acts by 1."
sourceIssues.correction:
The proof needs the following, all of which can be supplied by standard arguments.
(a) Realise the Lyndon sequence as the Ext_G(−, O/ϖ^n) sequence of 0 → C_1(T) → C_0(T) → Z → 0, where T is the Bruhat–Tits tree at x. Then U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is induced by the G-endomorphism T_1 of C_1 ≅ Z[G/Γ^1_0(x)] that sends an edge to the N(x)^2 edges two steps from it. There is a unique G-endomorphism T_0 of C_0 with ∂T_1 = T_0∂: A(v) = v − N·S_1(v) + S_2(v) on one vertex type and B(w) = S_1(w) − N·w on the other. On the Γ^1-terms this is the 2×2 Hecke matrix [[T_x^2 − N, −N T_x],[T_x, −N]], i.e. U_x^2 on oldforms. Its augmentation is 1, so the sequence is equivariant and the un-normalised double coset acts on both H^*(G)-terms by 1. With the paper's 1/N(x)^2 normalisation, U_{x^2} therefore acts on H^*(G) by N(x)^{-2}, not by 1 as printed. This is harmless because N(x) ≡ 1 mod p, so U_{x^2} − N(x)^{-2} is a unit exactly when U_{x^2} − 1 is.
(b) For general x: the operator diag(ϖ_x, ϖ_x^{-1}) ∈ SL_2(F_x) preserves components, and the same tree argument applies to each component's S-arithmetic group. Its two vertex stabilisers are the Γ^1-lattices of the components paired by [x], as in [6, §4.1.4].
(c) Also needed: the Φ-invariants and T^an-localisation bookkeeping behind "repeat this argument for each lattice Γ_i".
sourceIssues.reason:
1. I rendered pp. 416–418 and transcribed the text above. The v2 text is the same, so this is not a bracket defect.

2. The proof asserts equivariance of the whole Lyndon/Mayer–Vietoris sequence, including the connecting map H^{i-1}(Γ^1_0(x)) → H^i(G). It never defines U_{x^2} on H^*(Γ^1)^2 or on H^*(G). Its only justification is that g ∈ G, so "the corresponding map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2". What this argument actually proves is U_{x^2}∘res^G_{Γ_0} = res^G_{Γ_0}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^i(G) → H^i(Γ^1)^2 → H^i(Γ_0) is res − res = 0.

3. I checked from scratch which action the sequence really carries. G = Γ^1 *_{Γ^1_0} Γ^1 acts on the (q+1)-regular tree with quotient one edge. The sequence comes from 0 → Z[E] → Z[V] → Z → 0 via Ext_G(−, M), using Shapiro for compact induction. The Hecke operator T is the G-endomorphism of Z[E] described in the correction, and its image T(e) has q^2 terms. A G-equivariant lift T_V to Z[V] with T_V∂ = ∂T must be a finite combination of distance spheres. Solving the coefficient equations forces T_V(v0) = v0 − qS_1(v0) + S_2(v0) and T_V(v1) = −qv1 + S_1(v1). The lift is unique because G has no nonzero invariants in Z[V]. Using the other translation direction gives the mirror formulas. In both cases εT_V(v0) = 1 − q(q+1) + q(q+1) = 1 and εT_V(v1) = −q + (q+1) = 1. By naturality of connecting maps, δ∘T = δ, so T acts on H^*(G) by 1, not by N(x)^2.

4. A python check on tree balls for q = 2, 3, 4 confirms ∂T = T_V∂ and ε∘T_V = 1 (tree.py in my agent folder).

5. A degree-0 sanity check with trivial coefficients: T acts on H^0(Γ_0) by q^2. On H^0(Γ^1)^2 the lift gives the matrix [[1+q(q+1), −q(q+1)], [q+1, −q]], whose eigenvalues are 1 (on the diagonal, which is the image of H^0(G)) and q^2.

6. No other equivariant structure can give N(x)^2 on H^*(G) in general. It would need (N(x)^2 − 1)δ = 0, which fails for O/ϖ^m once m is large relative to the Taylor–Wiles level.

7. So the printed claim "U_{x^2} acts by 1" is literally wrong by the unit N(x)^{-2} ≡ 1 mod p, and the equivariance it rests on is asserted, not shown. The conclusion still holds, because only invertibility mod ϖ is used and α_x ≢ ±1.

8. The restriction to x trivial in the ray class group is acknowledged and the general case is waved at [6, §4.1.4]. I could not consult [6], which is cited as a Calegari–Venkatesh preprint.

Overall the candidate's description (equivariance asserted, not shown; the general case of x only sketched) is accurate. Lemma 9.6 itself is not in doubt. Defence first.
- The lemma is true, and the authors flag the argument as "implicit in … Chapter 4 of [6]".
- They explicitly reduce to x trivial in the ray class group and point to [6, §4.1.4] for the general case, which is indeed only notational (see (b)).
- The equivariance also holds. I checked the chain-level identity ∂T_1(e) = B(v_1) − A(v_0) by script on (N+1)-regular trees for N = 2, 3, 4, for both the forward and the backward double coset. It holds, with aug A = aug B = 1 and exactly N^2 edges in T_1(e).

The objection still stands, for two reasons.
1. The paper never defines the U_{x^2}-action on the middle term H^*(Γ^1)^2 and never proves that the maps of the sequence commute with it. The one justification it gives ("g ∈ G, so the map on H^*(G) is multiplication by the degree N(x)^2") computes [KgK]∘res^G_{Γ^1_0(x)}. That is not a map in the sequence: the composite H^*(G) → H^*(Γ^1)^2 → H^*(Γ^1_0(x)) is zero.
2. That justification also gives the wrong scalar. By naturality of the connecting map for the endomorphism (T_1, T_0, id_Z), δ∘[KgK] = δ. So on the image of δ the compatible scalar is 1 for the un-normalised operator, i.e. N(x)^{-2} for the paper's U_{x^2}. This differs from the printed 1 in O/ϖ^n whenever ϖ^n does not divide N(x)^2 − 1. It is harmless for the localisation, since N(x) ≡ 1 mod p.

So the key step is asserted without an adequate proof, and the stated result is not in doubt. The general-x case and the per-component and Φ bookkeeping are only sketched, but they are routine.

Consequences: Lemma 9.6 is cited nowhere else. Only Remark 9.8 discusses it. Theorems 9.19, 5.16 and 1.1 assume Conjecture B in full (including part 5) for each Q_N. The gap therefore affects only this proof.

The candidate's correction is right. I have made it concrete: the explicit T_0, and the scalar N(x)^{-2}. Separate items, not this one: the index slip H^{i−1}(G) → H^i(Γ^1)^2 in the displayed sequence (X-K9-15), and the normalisation issues (H-part2-17). This is not one of the 47 bracket errors.
